title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: We study this interaction directly. Our setup is not adversarial in the traditional sense: the distractor sentence explicitly instructs the model to ignore it, and the target question is unchanged in English. Any response degradation therefore reflects the model’s inability to maintain language-consistent instruction following when the prompt context contains unexpected script boundaries, a realistic failure mode in RAG and document-processing pipelines. To specifically isolate the script-boundary mechanism, we include Spanish as a control condition: sharing the Latin script with English, it separates script-boundary interference from language-identity interference. Strikingly, the model most vulnerable to this failure is not the weakest multilingual model but the strongest. This is consistent with what has been termed themultilingual curse, where richer multilingual pretraining can introduce cross-lingual interference that degrades output language control rather than improving it. Our contributions are three-fold: 1. We introduceMultilingual Distractor Interference (MDI), a lightweight, reproducible evaluation protocol for probing factual robustness under mixed-language prompt contamination. 2.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: We introduceMultilingual Distractor Interference (MDI), a lightweight, reproducible evaluation protocol for probing factual robustness under mixed-language prompt contamination. 2. We identify and quantify ametric confoundin exact-match-based hallucination scoring: for Llama-3.1-8B under Hindi distraction, 120 of 148 script-switched responses that were correct under clean conditions are semantically correct answers written in the wrong script, reducing the raw hallucination proxy from 0.710 to an adjusted semantic hallucination rate of 0.470. 3. We characterize afailure mode taxonomy: script-switching hallucination, abstention escalation, and stability, showing that the operative mode is determined by model-specific spontaneous generative capacity in the distractor language. The clean dissociation across five models with identical inputs is itself the finding: it rules out general prompt sensitivity and points to a tractable, model-level mechanism. 2

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Multilingual evaluation.Established multilingual benchmarks such as XTREME [Hu et al., 2020] and XGLUE [Liang et al., 2020] evaluate models on tasks presented in a target language, measuring cross-lingual transfer and per-language performance. Open-domain multilingual QA benchmarks such as MKQA [Longpre et al., 2021] similarly assume that task language and prompt language are aligned. Our setup differs fundamentally: the task remains English throughout; the foreign language appears only as prompt contamination. This distinction matters because it isolates instruction-following robustness from cross-lingual comprehension ability, a dimension that per-language benchmarks do not probe. Robustness to distracting context.Jia and Liang [2017] showed that prepending adversarial sentences to reading comprehension passages substantially degraded model accuracy; subsequent work extended this to extractive and generative QA settings. These studies focus on semantically relevant or adversarially crafted distractors within a single language.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: These studies focus on semantically relevant or adversarially crafted distractors within a single language. We study semantically irrelevant distractors that differ from the question in script and language, with an explicit ignore instruction, making any failure a clear case of instruction-following breakdown rather than comprehension difficulty. Muennighoff et al. [2023] show that instruction-following degrades when instructions and content appear in different languages, which is consistent with our finding that script-boundary crossing in the prompt context disrupts English output generation. Multilingual contamination in RAG.Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines frequently surface passages in languages other than the query language, particularly for cross-lingual or low-resource queries [Asai et al., 2024]. While prior work has examined multilingual retrieval quality and cross-lingual passage selection [Longpre et al., 2021], systematic study of how mixed-language retrieved passages affect generator output behavior rather than retrieval ranking has been limited.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: While prior work has examined multilingual retrieval quality and cross-lingual passage selection [Longpre et al., 2021], systematic study of how mixed-language retrieved passages affect generator output behavior rather than retrieval ranking has been limited. Our wiki_para ablation (Section 5.5) provides a controlled analog: a monolingual English paragraph prepended to a factual question, isolating the effect of contextual format confusion from scriptswitching. Hallucination and factuality metrics.Exact-match scoring is known to be an imperfect proxy for semantic correctness in monolingual settings [Joshi et al., 2017]; we show it introduces a systematic directional bias in multilingual settings. For models with strong spontaneous generation in the distractor language, exact-match conflates script-switched but semantically correct responses with genuine hallucinations, inflating apparent error rates in a way that depends on the model’s generative profile rather than its factual accuracy.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: MDI is a lightweight evaluation protocol that probes whether semantically irrelevant foreign-language context disrupts English factual question answering. The key design choice is that the distractor is not adversarial: it explicitly declares itself irrelevant and instructs the model to ignore it. Any response degradation therefore reflects a failure of language-grounded instruction following rather than a failure of comprehension. The model understood the question but could not maintain English output in the presence of a foreign-script context. This makes MDI a clean probe for a specific and practically relevant robustness dimension. MDI requires no new data collection, annotation, or model access beyond standard inference, making it straightforwardly applicable to any instruction-tuned model evaluated on existing factual QA benchmarks.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Each question is evaluated under eight distractor conditions: •clean: no distractor; establishes the per-model baseline. •es/es_long: a Spanish sentence repeated once or three times. •hi/hi_long: a Hindi sentence in Devanagari script, repeated once or three times. •zh / zh_long: a Chinese sentence in Simplified Chinese script, repeated once or three times. 3 •wiki_para : a paragraph-length English Wikipedia excerpt, included as an ablation to isolate context-length and format-confusion effects from script-switching. The three distractor languages were selected to vary along two dimensions relevant to the hypothesized failure mechanism: script and pretraining resource level. Spanish uses the Latin script shared with English, providing a baseline condition where script boundaries are absent and any interference must arise from language identity alone. Hindi (Devanagari script) and Chinese (Simplified Chinese script) both introduce a non-Latin script boundary, but differ substantially in pretraining corpus size: Chinese is among the highest-resource non-English languages in most LLM pretraining corpora, while Hindi is comparatively lower-resource.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Hindi (Devanagari script) and Chinese (Simplified Chinese script) both introduce a non-Latin script boundary, but differ substantially in pretraining corpus size: Chinese is among the highest-resource non-English languages in most LLM pretraining corpora, while Hindi is comparatively lower-resource. This contrast allows us to test whether the failure mode is driven by script-switching propensity specifically or by distractor language resource level more generally, a distinction that proves consequential in Section 5.4. The base distractor for each language is a single sentence that declares itself irrelevant and instructs the model to ignore it. For example, the Spanish distractor reads:“Nota: Este texto no tiene relación con la pregunta. Por favor ignóralo. ”Hindi and Chinese equivalents are constructed analogously in their respective native scripts. The long variants repeat the base sentence three times to test whether distractor length modulates the observed effects.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: The long variants repeat the base sentence three times to test whether distractor length modulates the observed effects. The wiki_para condition uses a fixed paragraph sampled from the WikiText-2 training split (minimum 200 characters) as a realistic approximation of a retrieved English passage. In all conditions, the distractor is prepended to the question with a blank line separator.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: For TruthfulQA, each item is presented as a four-choice multiple-choice question. The system prompt instructs the model to respond with a single letter (A-D); accuracy is measured by log-probability scoring over the four option tokens, requiring no generation. This format structurally prevents script-switching and serves as a format-controlled upper bound on robustness. For TriviaQA, each item is presented as an open-ended short-answer question. The system prompt instructs the model to respond with a short phrase only, and specifies“If you do not know, say: I don’t know. ”to elicit calibrated abstention. All TriviaQA generation uses greedy decoding (T=0 , maximum 32 new tokens).

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: TruthfulQA.Accuracy is reported, defined as the proportion of questions where the highestprobability option is correct. TriviaQA.Four metrics are reported: (i)exact-match accuracy, evaluated against the full gold alias list; (ii)abstention rate, detected by substring match on “I don’t know,” “unknown,” and related phrases; (iii)hallucination proxy rate, defined as the proportion of responses that are neither correct nor abstaining, such that accuracy + abstention + hallucination proxy = 1; and (iv)script-switching rate, the proportion of outputs containing at least one character from the distractor’s native script, detected via Unicode block membership (Devanagari for Hindi; CJK Unified Ideographs for Chinese). The hallucination proxy is an intentionally conservative operationalization of confident factual error. As we show in Section 5.3, it conflates script-switched but semantically correct responses with genuine semantic errors in multilingual settings, and must be decomposed accordingly.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: As we show in Section 5.3, it conflates script-switched but semantically correct responses with genuine semantic errors in multilingual settings, and must be decomposed accordingly. Statistical testing.Pairwise comparisons between each distractor condition and the clean baseline use McNemar’s test on paired binary outcomes with continuity correction, with 95% confidence intervals computed via bootstrap resampling (n=2000).

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: 4.1 Models. We evaluate five publicly available instruction-tuned models spanning four training lineages and two parameter scales (Table 1). Model selection was guided by three criteria. First,family diversity: Meta 4 Llama, Microsoft Phi, Mistral AI, and Alibaba Qwen represent independent pretraining pipelines with different multilingual data compositions, allowing failure mode differences to be attributed to training rather than shared architectural choices. Second,scale coverage: the 3-3.8B and 7-8B ranges are representative of widely deployed open-source models that fit within single-GPU inference budgets in float16 precision, enabling exact replication without proprietary access. Third,controlled intra-family comparison: Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.2-3B share the same tokenizer, so any behavioral difference between them under identical distractor conditions cannot be attributed to tokenizer fragmentation, isolating model capacity and pretraining exposure as the operative variables. title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: We evaluate on TruthfulQA [Lin et al., 2022] and TriviaQA [Joshi et al., 2017], chosen for their complementary evaluation formats. TruthfulQA’s multiple-choice structure permits log-probability scoring over single option tokens without any generation step, providing a format-controlled baseline in which script-switching is structurally impossible. TriviaQA’s open short-answer format exposes generation behavior directly, allowing observation of script-switching, abstention, and hallucination under distractor conditions. Together, the two datasets allow us to separate failure modes that arise from the generation process from those that arise from answer selection, a distinction that is central to interpreting our results. For TruthfulQA we use the mc1 split from the validation set, sampling 500 questions with a fixed random seed (seed = 42). For TriviaQA we use theunfiltered.nocontext configuration from the validation split, sampling 500 questions with the same seed; answers are evaluated against the full alias list provided in the dataset.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Each model is evaluated on every question under every distractor condition, yielding: 5models× 2datasets×8conditions×500questions= 40,000evaluations. Question-distractor pairings are fixed across models so that all comparisons are paired, enabling McNemar’s test for significance testing throughout. 5 Results. 5.1 TruthfulQA: Multiple-Choice Is Robust. TruthfulQA accuracy is unaffected by single-sentence multilingual distractors for all models (Table 2). No accuracy drop is statistically significant under single-sentence conditions (p >0.05 , McNemar’s test). The insulation of TruthfulQA from single-sentence distractors follows directly from its format: logprobability scoring over single letter tokens removes the generation step that makes script-switching possible. This makes TruthfulQA MC accuracy an unreliable signal in either direction under distractor conditions, a methodological point for future benchmark design. 5 Table 2: TruthfulQA accuracy: clean baseline and worst distractor condition. 95% CIs via bootstrap (n=2000).ns: not significant; ∗∗p<0.01; ∗∗∗p<0.001.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
section: 5.3 The Metric Confound: Unpacking the Hallucination Proxy
text: The remaining 28 cases within this 148-response subset (18.9%) are genuine semantic errors: wrong proper nouns or semantically incorrect paraphrases. Accounting for the 120 script-switched responses identified as semantically correct, the adjusted semantic hallucination rate is 235/500 = 0.470, compared to a raw hallucination proxy of 0.710 and a clean baseline of 0.416. The primary consequence of script-switching isoutput in the wrong language, not fabricated content, though a meaningful real increase in semantic errors (+5.4 pp) remains. The implication for evaluation practice is direct: exact-match-based hallucination metrics in multilingual settings should be decomposed into script-switched (potentially semantically correct) and genuinely wrong components. Reporting raw exact-match failure for a model like Llama-3.1-8B in mixed-language conditions overstates semantic hallucination by a factor of approximately 1.5×. Benchmark comparisons between multilingual and English-primary models may hence systematically understate the reliability gap in contexts where the multilingual model is more likely to script-switch.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Two comparisons rule out alternative explanations for the Llama-3.1-8B dissociation. Hindi vs. Chinese.Chinese is a higher-resource language than Hindi in most LLM pretraining corpora. If distractor language resource level drove the effect, Llama-3.1-8B should show an equal or stronger hallucination spike under the Chinese distractor. It does not: CJK-script outputs occur on 0% of responses, and the hallucination rate falls slightly to 0.382 ( ∆ =−0.034 , p= 0.009 ). The model has sufficient Hindi generative capacity to switch into Devanagari output spontaneously, but not Chinese. 7 Llama-3.1-8B vs. Llama-3.2-3B.Both models share the same tokenizer, ruling out tokenizer fragmentation as the driver. Yet Llama-3.2-3B produces Devanagari on only 1.2% of responses under the same Hindi distractor. The relevant variable is not tokenization, and not instructed generation ability (both models can produce Devanagari when explicitly asked to do so), but spontaneous script-switching propensity under distractor conditions.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: The relevant variable is not tokenization, and not instructed generation ability (both models can produce Devanagari when explicitly asked to do so), but spontaneous script-switching propensity under distractor conditions. This propensity appears to be a function of model scale and pretraining Hindi exposure, and it is concentrated in the larger model, not the smaller one. This last point is counterintuitive and practically important:stronger multilingual capacity does not protect against this failure mode; for models with strong spontaneous generation in the distractor language, it produces it.This is consistent with what has been termed themultilingual curse, the observation that incorporating more languages during pretraining can introduce crosslingual interference that degrades target-language behavior [Muennighoff et al., 2023]. Here the interference manifests not as degraded comprehension but as degraded output language control: the model understands the English question but cannot suppress generation in the language whose script dominates the prompt context.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Here the interference manifests not as degraded comprehension but as degraded output language control: the model understands the English question but cannot suppress generation in the language whose script dominates the prompt context. The implication is that models with the richest multilingual pretraining may be the most susceptible to this specific failure mode, not the least.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: The wiki_para condition produces a qualitatively different and cross-model consistent effect: nearuniversal abstention (Mistral-7B: 0.860; Qwen-2.5-3B: 0.998; even Llama-3.1-8B, which shows minimal abstention under Hindi, abstains on 80.6% of wiki_para questions). This is not a scriptswitching effect as the paragraph is English, but a context-format confusion: models appear to treat the prepended paragraph as part of the question context and decline to answer when the “passage” does not contain the answer, as if performing reading comprehension rather than open-domain QA. This is directly relevant to RAG deployments, and to a gap in how RAG systems are currently evaluated. Most existing evaluation of RAG systems focuses on retrieval quality and answer accuracy over clean, language-matched passages; systematic evaluation over mixed-language or contextually mismatched retrieved context has been limited. Our results suggest that such mismatches can cause widespread abstention independent of retrieval quality. A model that retrieves the correct passage but treats it as reading comprehension context will abstain rather than answer.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: A model that retrieves the correct passage but treats it as reading comprehension context will abstain rather than answer. This is a failure mode that is invisible to retrieval-focused evaluation metrics but consequential in deployment. Evaluation protocols for multilingual RAG should therefore include conditions where retrieved passages are in a different language or format than the query, and should track abstention rates alongside answer accuracy.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Repeating the single-sentence distractor three times produces modest additional degradation but does not change the qualitative pattern. For Llama-3.1-8B, hi_long hallucination proxy is 0.704 vs. 0.710 for hi, essentially unchanged. For Qwen-2.5-3B, abstention rises from 0.730 to 0.842 under hi_long. The failure mode taxonomy established under single-sentence conditions is stable under distractor repetition. 6 Discussion. Why does Llama-3.1-8B switch to Devanagari?The pattern is consistent with a model that has learned strong Hindi text generation during pretraining and whose instruction-following mechanism is insufficient to suppress spontaneous language switching when a Devanagari-script context is present. Crucially, the relevant capacity isspontaneousrather than instructed: all five models in our evaluation can produce Devanagari output when explicitly instructed to do so, but only Llama-3.1-8B switches scripts without such instruction under distractor conditions.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Crucially, the relevant capacity isspontaneousrather than instructed: all five models in our evaluation can produce Devanagari output when explicitly instructed to do so, but only Llama-3.1-8B switches scripts without such instruction under distractor conditions. The 8B/3B contrast within the Llama family, with identical tokenizers but different scale and pretraining data exposure, suggests that the failure mode scales with multilingual capacity in a way that is not obvious from standard multilingual benchmarks. We do not have access to training data composition to make this definitive. 8 A failure mode taxonomy.Our results support three response modes under multilingual distractor text: (1)script-switching hallucination: confident generation in the wrong language, inflating exactmatch error; (2)abstention escalation: rising “I don’t know” rates with no hallucination increase; and (3)stability: no significant change in either direction. Which mode a model exhibits in open-answer settings depends on whether it has spontaneous generative capacity in the distractor language, not on distractor length, language resource level, or tokenizer characteristics.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Which mode a model exhibits in open-answer settings depends on whether it has spontaneous generative capacity in the distractor language, not on distractor length, language resource level, or tokenizer characteristics. A fourth route to apparent stability is format constraint: TruthfulQA’s multiple-choice scoring removes the generation step entirely, suppressing the failure mode regardless of the model’s multilingual profile. Implications for evaluation.Current multilingual robustness evaluations focus on per-language task performance. Our results suggest that a different dimension is both practically important and poorly captured by existing protocols: the effect of foreign-language prompt context on otherwise English tasks.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Our results suggest that a different dimension is both practically important and poorly captured by existing protocols: the effect of foreign-language prompt context on otherwise English tasks. More concretely: (i) hallucination proxy rates computed via exact-match in mixedlanguage settings should be reported alongside script-switching rates and adjusted semantic error rates; (ii) models explicitly optimized for multilingual instruction following should be evaluated specifically for output language control under mixed-script prompt conditions, as stronger multilingual capacity appears to increase rather than decrease susceptibility to this failure mode; (iii) RAG evaluation benchmarks should include mixed-language retrieved context, as even English-language paragraph noise produces widespread abstention. More broadly, these findings suggest that multilingual pretraining objectives and data composition have consequences for output language control that are not captured by standard cross-lingual transfer benchmarks: a dimension that warrants explicit attention in multilingual model development. Limitations.Our experimental choices reflect deliberate scope decisions appropriate for a diagnostic probe.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Limitations.Our experimental choices reflect deliberate scope decisions appropriate for a diagnostic probe. All models are evaluated at realistic single-GPU inference budgets in float16 precision, reflecting conditions under which these models are actually deployed rather than idealized research settings. The distractor sentences explicitly declare themselves irrelevant by design: this isolates instruction-following failure from comprehension failure, making the probe interpretable rather than weaker. More naturalistic contamination without an ignore instruction is important future work and may produce larger effects. We evaluate five open-source models; the pattern may not generalize to closed-source models or models with different pretraining data mixes, and we encourage replication of MDI across a broader model population. Our model set consists of models released between 2023 and 2024 and therefore does not include the latest generations of open-source instruction-tuned LLMs. We view replication across current-generation models as an important direction for future work. Abstention detection via substring matching may miss non-standard refusal formulations, particularly Mistral-7B’s more discursive refusals.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: We introduce Multilingual Distractor Interference (MDI) and use it to identify a systematic metric confound in exact-match-based hallucination scoring: for models with strong spontaneous Hindi generative capacity, a Hindi-language distractor triggers script-switching rather than semantic hallucination, and exact-match scoring cannot distinguish the two. Review of all 291 script-switched responses finds that, among the 148 cases that were correct under clean conditions, 120 (81.1%) are semantically correct answers in the wrong script, reducing the raw hallucination proxy from 0.710 to an adjusted semantic hallucination rate of 0.470. Models without this spontaneous capacity respond through abstention escalation instead, a less severe but equally systematic failure mode with different practical consequences. Paragraph-length English distractors produce a third mode: near-universal abstention consistent with reading-comprehension confusion, with direct implications for RAG evaluation.

title: Output Language Confusion under Multilingual Prompt Contamination
text: Paragraph-length English distractors produce a third mode: near-universal abstention consistent with reading-comprehension confusion, with direct implications for RAG evaluation. The takeaway for practitioners is two-fold: (1) deploy-time failure mode in mixed-language pipelines depends on the model’s spontaneous generative profile; and (2) exact-match hallucination metrics reported for models with strong non-English generation should be treated as upper bounds requiring script-switch decomposition before interpretation. More broadly, our results suggest that output language control under mixed-script prompt conditions is a distinct and underexamined axis of multilingual model quality, and one that should be evaluated explicitly alongside cross-lingual transfer and per-language accuracy as multilingual models continue to scale. 9

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: An email assistant should not complete less work simply because a user phrases the same request differently. Yet most benchmarks test each task with only one canonical request, leaving this form of robustness largely unmeasured. We test whether email assistants remain reliable when the requested information, available evidence, and expected outcome stay fixed, but the communication style or English variety changes. We construct validated variants along five communication-style axes and four rule-based dialect conditions, and evaluate them on three benchmarks: a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline and two tool-using agents. Indirect requests reduce performance on all three benchmarks, while formal requests reduce performance on both agentic benchmarks. Examining the systems more closely shows that these failures have different causes. Verbose requests mainly hurt a lexical retriever by making the relevant email harder to find. By contrast, indirect and dialect variants remain harmful even when the relevant email is retrieved. In the agentic setting, indirect and formal requests mainly cause the agents to omit required actions, not to take more unsupported actions. These results show that a successful response is not enough to establish robustness: evaluations should vary how requests are expressed and separately measure whether agents complete the requested work.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: An email assistant should not complete less work because a user asks indirectly, writes formally, adds surrounding context, or uses a different variety of English. These differences are common in real communication, but they do not necessarily change what the user wants. If the requested information, relevant evidence, named entities, and intended outcome remain the same, a reliable assistant should return the same answer or carry out the same actions. Current evaluations rarely test this expectation. Most benchmarks represent each task with one canonical request, even though the same task can be expressed in many ways. Prior work shows that semantically equivalent query formulations can change retrieval results, including for recent retrieval architectures [Penha et al., 2022, Hagen et al., 2024], and that linguistic reformulation affects both retrieval and answer generation in retrieval-augmented question answering [Cao et al., 2026]. Performance also varies across systematic varieties of English [Ziems et al., 2022, 2023, Sap et al., 2019, Srirag et al., 2025].

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Performance also varies across systematic varieties of English [Ziems et al., 2022, 2023, Sap et al., 2019, Srirag et al., 2025]. These findings establish that wording matters for finding and answering information, but they leave an important question for interactive agents: can a change in wording alter whether the requested work is completed? This question matters because an agent can fail without producing an obviously bad response. An assistant may identify the task, call some appropriate tools, and reply fluently while still omitting an action needed to finish the request. Conversely, it may retrieve the wrong evidence or take an unsupported action. These failures require different responses from system designers, but a single end-to-end success score does not distinguish them. Diagnostic agent benchmarks similarly show that aggregate scores can combine failures such as skipping a required tool, ignoring a tool result, or producing unsupported output [Kokane et al., 2024, Soni, arXiv:2610.02627v1 [cs.AI] 2 Oct 2026 2026].

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Diagnostic agent benchmarks similarly show that aggregate scores can combine failures such as skipping a required tool, ignoring a tool result, or producing unsupported output [Kokane et al., 2024, Soni, arXiv:2610.02627v1 [cs.AI] 2 Oct 2026 2026]. Robustness evaluation should therefore ask not only whether performance changes, but what the system stopped doing correctly. We study whether email assistants remain reliable when the same request is expressed in different ways. We evaluate the two settings for email assistants: theretrieval-augmented generation(RAG) setting, where the system retrieves evidence from the archive and answers from it, and theagentic setting, where the system calls tools to carry out the request. Covering both lets us examine whether communication variation affects the information an assistant returns as well as the actions it performs. We vary communication style and English variety while keeping the underlying task and expected outcome unchanged, and validate the resulting requests to ensure that they preserve the original intent.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: We vary communication style and English variety while keeping the underlying task and expected outcome unchanged, and validate the resulting requests to ensure that they preserve the original intent. Our work makes three contributions: • A framework for generating validated request variants.Figure 1 shows it. An LLM rewriter produces the communication-style poles and a rule-based transducer produces the dialect varieties, and a set of gates admits a variant only once it still requests the information or action asked for, carries the relevant task details, and expects the same outcome. • An evaluation spanning RAG and agentic settings.We apply the framework to email question answering and to tool-using agents, so that the same variation can be traced through retrieval, answering, and execution. • A closer analysis of assistant failures.We examine not only whether performance changes, but also whether failures come from finding the wrong information, producing an incorrect answer, omitting required actions, or taking unsupported actions.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: We evaluate whether a system fulfills the same request when the request is expressed differently. We consider two forms of variation.Communication stylechanges how a writer presents a request. Dialectchanges grammatical and dialectal features according to patterns documented for varieties of English. Figure 1 shows how a variant is built and follows one request through a RAG pipeline. 2.1 Variation Taxonomy. 2.1.1 Communication-Style Axes. The five axes and the definition of each pole are listed in Table 1. Each style axis pairs areference pole, a plain rewrite that carries no marked style, with acontrastivepole that carries the property under test. Formality is the exception: neither a formal nor a casual register is neutral, so both of its poles are contrastive.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Formality is the exception: neither a formal nor a casual register is neutral, so both of its poles are contrastive. Each axis rests on a documented distinction: directness on the contrast between on-record and off-record requests [Brown and Levinson, 1987, Mannekote et al., 2025]; formality on register variation [Pavlick and Tetreault, 2016, Rao and Tetreault, 2018]; verbosity on evidence that input length and the position of the relevant information affect model behavior [Levy et al., 2024, Liu et al., 2024]; emotion on evidence that emotional framing changes behavior on an otherwise fixed task [Li et al., 2023, Sharma et al., 2024]; and grammaticality on reported sensitivity to grammatical form [Cao et al., 2026] and on work measuring encoder robustness to grammatical error [Yin et al., 2020]. Appendix A describes each axis in full.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: We evaluate four varieties: Indian English, Colloquial Singapore English, Black South African English, and Nigerian English. Dialect differs from the non-grammatical pole in both source and interpretation. The non-grammatical pole is a constructed set of learner-like slips deliberately detached from any speech community, whereas the dialect conditions apply features documented for particular varieties. The variants are synthetic stress tests rather than samples of how individual speakers write, and every claim we make concerns system behavior rather than speakers. 2.2 Variant Construction. title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Across a base query and all of its variants we hold fixed the information need or requested action, the supporting evidence, named entities, numbers, dates, protected literals, and the expected outcome. Only the wording may differ. A candidate enters the evaluation set only after clearing every gate that applies to its pole. A deterministicfactual gaterequires the variant to be non-empty, to differ from the original, and to preserve every numeric token and protected literal. Anintent gate, a rubric judge ( gpt-5.4, temperature 0.0), asks whether the variant requests exactly the same information. This gate is what protects the paired design: a variant that clears it is still answerable by the same gold answer, so a difference in outcome cannot be a difference in task.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: This gate is what protects the paired design: a variant that clears it is still answerable by the same gold answer, so a difference in outcome cannot be a difference in task. Astyle gateasks whether the variant realizes its target pole, given that pole’s operational definition from Table 1; for dialect it instead requires at least two features documented in the electronic World Atlas of Varieties of English to have changed [Kortmann et al., 2013]. Ahuman-likeness gateasks whether the text reads as something a person would type, which guards against rewrites that reach the style label while reading synthetic. It applies to four of the six contrastive poles except verbose and non-grammatical (prompts in Appendix E). Two authors independently labeled the same 120 variants, 20 per contrastive pole, answering the questions the gates ask. Agreement was complete on intent (κ=1.00), and reached 82.5%on style and80.0%on human-likeness.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: 3.1 Evaluation Tasks. We apply the framework to three tasks, one RAG task and two agentic benchmarks. EnronQA (RAG).Retrieval-augmented question answering over a personal email archive Ryan et al. [2025]. We sample 400 questions from the training split under an isolated-axes design: four bins of 100, where each complex bin flips exactly one complexity property against thesimplecontrol. The three complex bins are3-hop(three or more reasoning hops),multi-question(the question asks for two or more distinct things), andthreaded(resolution depends on earlier messages in the thread)(detail in Appendix B). Holding the other two properties at their control setting is what makes the per-bin breakdown of §4.2.1 attributable to one property rather than to overall difficulty. Each question is paired with a gold answer and the gold email that contains it, and retrieval runs over the target user’s own inbox. ToolTalk (Agentic).A multi-turn tool-using benchmark [Farn and Shin, 2023]. We use thehard split: 50 conversations comprising 194 user turns over 28 tool APIs.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: We use thehard split: 50 conversations comprising 194 user turns over 28 tool APIs. Grading compares the agent’s calls against ground-truth API calls. The harness is teacher-forced: the conversation is rebuilt from the gold trajectory and the databases are reset before each assistant turn, so an error on one turn cannot propagate to the next. WorkBench (Agentic).A sandbox benchmark of workplace tasks across five domains [Styles et al., 2024]. We use its 90-task email domain, the subset solvable with the email toolkit alone, and expose all 26 tools on every task so that the agent must still select among them. Grading is by database state: a task is correct only if executing the agent’s predicted calls leaves the sandbox in the ground-truth state, which makes the metric binary and unforgiving of a single wrong argument. We report task accuracy.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Retrieval.EnronQA is run with three retrievers over the same corpus, all returning the top k=5 emails. BM25 is lexical ( rank_bm25) and indexes the full text of every email [Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009]. SPLADE is learned-sparse (naver/splade-v3), producing term-weight vectors scored by dot product [Formal et al., 2021]. BGE-M3 is dense (BAAI/bge-m3) [Chen et al., 2024]. 4 Both neural retrievers truncate to 512 tokens. Retrieval is identical within a retriever, so any difference between answerers under a fixed retriever is a generation difference. We use SPLADE as the headline retriever because it provides the strongest baseline retrieval among the tested systems. Answering and grading.We evaluate three models: gpt-5.6-terra, gpt-5.4-mini, and Kimi-K2.6. All headline results use gpt-5.6-terra, which is run on all three benchmarks.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: All headline results use gpt-5.6-terra, which is run on all three benchmarks. The cross-model comparison of §4.3 is restricted to EnronQA and ToolTalk: running the full ten-pole grid on WorkBench for the two additional models was beyond the compute available, so that benchmark is reported on the headline model alone and the coverage actually obtained is stated in Table 6 so that what is missing is explicit. On EnronQA each model receives the retrieved emails and the question and is instructed to answer in one sentence using only the information in the email. Each agent condition is repeated withK=3 replicates whose per-scenario metrics are averaged before any test. Answers on EnronQA are graded bygpt-5.4 at temperature 0, which sees the email, the question, the gold answer, and the candidate answer and returns a single-line judgement.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Each task has its own success metric, so a percentage point is not the same quantity across benchmarks and magnitudes should not be compared between columns. EnronQA reports judged answer accuracy, and additionally Recall@5, the rate at which the gold email appears in the retrieved set. ToolTalk reports conversation success, which requires every ground-truth call to be matched with no incorrect action, along with recall of required calls, precision, and the incorrect-action rate. WorkBench reports task accuracy against the ground-truth sandbox state, and additionally the F1 between predicted and ground-truth tool calls, the rate at which no tool call is issued, and the rate at which execution leaves an unwanted change to the sandbox.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Every variant is compared against the base item on the items present in both conditions. Detail shows in Appendix G. For EnronQA, each item yields one binary outcome from a single run, so the paired difference is−1, 0 or +1 . We use the exact McNemar test on those pairs, which conditions on their number and is exact at any sample size. For the other two agent benchmarks, each condition is run K=3 times, so for itemi we average a metric over replicates before any test, then form the paired differencedi = ¯vi−¯ni against the base item. We test the mean of those differences with a paired percentile bootstrap over items, resampling item indices with replacementB=10,000 times under a fixed seed, reading the 95% interval off the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of the resampled means and a two-sidedp-value off the proportion of them falling either side of zero.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Two of the three complex bins are more fragile than the control. Contrastive rewrites break 4.26% of previously-correct slots on 3-hop questions and 4.08% on multi-question ones, against 1.62% on the simple control and 1.88% on threaded questions. Dialect variation follows the same ordering at a uniformly higher level, from 2.91% on threaded to 5.36% on multi-question (Table 9 and Figure 4 report how often a rewrite broke a question).

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: The agents can have two failure modes: the agent could take wrong actions, or it could take too few. Figure 3 separates them. On ToolTalk the effect is concentrated in a failure to complete required work. Required-call recall falls by−11.28 points under indirect, and−10.32 under formal (both p<.001). The incorrect-action rate moves in neither pole:+2.96(p=.14) and−1.94(p=.35). WorkBench shows the similar mechanism (Figure 3c; Table 17). Underformal the share of tasks with no tool calls rises from 0.4% to 12.2% (p<.001), while unwanted side effects fall from 8.9% to 4.8% (p=.027). Across both agentic benchmarks the poles that reduce task success reduce the amount of required work performed while leaving the rate of unsupported actions unchanged.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: 5.1 Request Explicitness Affects Performance. The most consistent communication-style effect is not the one that changes the most text, but hiding the main request in the query. Parsing every variant against its own original with a dependency parser [Honnibal et al., 2020] (Table 13), the indirect pole retains the head verb of the request as the main predicate least often on all three benchmarks, from 12.5% of slots on EnronQA down to 4.7% on WorkBench, and the formal pole is in the bottom three poles on all three. The two poles reach that position differently: the indirect pole deletes the original head verb in 16% to 40% of slots, whereas the formal pole retains it in 68% to 91% of slots but frequently places it in a subordinate clause. This pattern suggests that performance is influenced by changing how explicitly the request is expressed [Austin, 1975, Searle, 1975, Mannekote et al., 2025]. This pattern suggests that performance is influenced by changing how explicitly the request is expressed [Austin, 1975, Searle, 1975, Mannekote et al., 2025]. Recent evaluations report that models remain weaker at recovering indirect illocutionary force than at interpreting explicit requests [Koo et al., 2025, Solidjonov, 2026].

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
section: 5.2 Incomplete Fulfillment as an Agentic Failure Mode
text: An end-to-end success score combines two failures with different consequences: an agent can take an unwanted action, or it can omit an action that the request requires. For the indirect and formal poles, the dominant change is in the second type. Shown in both agentic settings, the affected agents complete less of the requested work without a corresponding increase in unsupported actions. The WorkBench trajectories show two routes into that outcome (Table 17). Underformal the agent more often never starts: the share of tasks with no tool call at all rises from 0.4% to 12.2% (p<.001), close to the−12.2 point accuracy loss. Under indirect that share moves only to 1.5% (p=.25), while the F1 between predicted and ground-truth calls falls−8.42 points (p<.001), so the agent acts but the calls land in the wrong state. This result complements work showing that aggregate success rates do not identify which tool-use failure occurred [Kokane et al., 2024, Soni, 2026]. title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Dialect variation reduces performance on all three benchmarks. Our finding of performance drops across English varieties is consistent with the disparities reported for language understanding [Ziems et al., 2022, 2023, Srirag et al., 2025], for social tasks such as hate-speech detection [Sap et al., 2019], and for model judgments about people [Hofmann et al., 2024]. The dialect transformations apply grammatical features documented for each variety, whereas the non-grammatical pole is a constructed set of slips produced by a language model, which suggests that variation beyond isolated grammatical slips carries part of the effect. It is worth noticing that dialect variants are generated at feature density 1.0, the attested upper bound, so this condition is a deliberate worst case.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
section: 5.4 Implications for Evaluation and System Design
text: Three implications can be derived from the results. First, a task should not be represented by a single canonical wording. Retrieval research has shown that results move under semantically equivalent query variation [Penha et al., 2022, Hagen et al., 2024], and Cao et al. [2026] reports the same fragility in the RAG setting. Our results extend that requirement to the agentic setting, where the same variation changes whether the requested work is carried out. Second, robustness evaluation should be stage-aware, because the same drop in a success score has different causes and therefore different fixes. Replacing BM25 with SPLADE removes most of the verbosity penalty at a comparable baseline. The indirect and dialect penalties persist when the gold evidence is retrieved.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
section: 5.4 Implications for Evaluation and System Design
text: The indirect and dialect penalties persist when the gold evidence is retrieved. Component-level measurement has to come before the choice of mitigation, and choosing a stronger model is not a substitute for it: the model with the highest baseline on both systems where all three models were run is also the one whose results move significantly in the most conditions. Third, completeness and unsupported action should be reported separately. Required-call recall, failure to act, and read-without-write behavior are computable from a trajectory without a gold final answer, so they can be monitored where end-state grading is unavailable. They are not a substitute for final grading, but they expose a failure that response quality and safety metrics miss, and they distinguish an agent that has become appropriately cautious from one that is quietly doing less of the requested work.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: We tested whether RAG-based and agentic assistants fulfill the same task when only the request’s communication style or English variety changes. Indirect requests produced the most consistent style loss; verbosity primarily disrupted lexical retrieval; and dialect sensitivity remained after accounting for whether the gold email was retrieved. Across the agentic benchmarks, indirect and formal requests mainly reduced completion of required actions. Evaluations should therefore vary request formulation, inspect intermediate retrieval and execution signals, and report required-action completion separately from unsupported action. Limitations There are several limitations in this work. First, dialect variants are generated at feature density 1.0 only, a deliberate worst case rather than an estimate of typical use. Second, the WorkBenchindirect pole passes only 64 of 90 slots, leading to lower coverage. Third, on ToolTalk theconcise reference pole moves−9.0 points, so the reference poles are an imperfect control there.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: The five axes summarized in Table 1 are described here in full. Directness.This axis separates an explicit request from one whose information need must be inferred. At the direct pole the request is stated as a question or command; at the indirect pole it is conveyed through a need, hint, observation, or expression of uncertainty. The contrast follows the distinction between on-record and off-record requests in Brown and Levinson [1987] and Mannekote et al. [2025]. Formality.This axis separates a polished professional register from a casual, chat-like one, following the register variation studied in Pavlick and Tetreault [2016] and Rao and Tetreault [2018]. Formality has been reported as a source of variation in retrieval-augmented question answering in Cao et al. [2026]. Verbosity.This axis separates a concise request from the same request embedded in additional text. The added material is generic chatter, hedging, or digression, and introduces no new fact about the task, the evidence, or the expected answer.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: The added material is generic chatter, hedging, or digression, and introduces no new fact about the task, the evidence, or the expected answer. Prior work suggests that input length and the position of the relevant information affect model behavior [Levy et al., 2024, Liu et al., 2024]. Emotion.This axis separates neutral wording from wording that expresses frustration, stress, anxiety, or urgency. Emotional content in a prompt is known to change model behavior on an otherwise fixed task [Li et al., 2023], and models have been shown to revise responses under user pressure [Sharma et al., 2024]. The axis tests whether that occurs when the task, evidence, and expected outcome are held constant. Grammaticality.This axis separates standard written English from understandable English carrying systematic grammatical deviation, including the topic or object fronted, the question word moved with the auxiliary dropped, the verb flattened with an adverb carrying the time, or clauses split and reordered.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Grammaticality.This axis separates standard written English from understandable English carrying systematic grammatical deviation, including the topic or object fronted, the question word moved with the auxiliary dropped, the verb flattened with an adverb carrying the time, or clauses split and reordered. Systematic slips sit on top of that restructuring, including dropped or wrong articles, missing plural marking, and tense or agreement errors. The pole is defined by properties of the text alone and is not conditioned on any writer attribute. B EnronQA Sampling Design EnronQA is the only benchmark in the study for which we choose the items, so the choice is described in full. The goal was a sample on which question complexity could be read as an effect of one property at a time rather than of overall difficulty.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: The goal was a sample on which question complexity could be read as an effect of one property at a time rather than of overall difficulty. Classification.Three complexity properties are assigned by a rule-based classifier over the question text alone: reasoning depth (1-hop, 2-hop, 3+-hop), scored from the presence of a context prefix, a relative clause, a nested reference to something mentioned elsewhere, and two or more clause connectives; question multiplicity (single-question, multi-question), triggered by coordinatingand, as well asoralong withthat introduce a new wh-clause; and context dependency ( self-contained, thread-dependent), triggered by explicit reference to an earlier or prior message. Broad threading markers such asforwardedorre:were deliberately excluded, since a message in a thread can still be self-answerable. A fourth label, reasoning type, is assigned from the question and gold answer under a fixed priority order: causal, comparative, aggregation, temporal, bridging, and otherwise extraction.

C Verbalized Sampling A single rewrite request per item produces low-diversity output: the model converges on one stock opener and reuses it across items, so the resulting variant set measures one phrasing rather than a style. We therefore generate each contrastive pole with verbalized sampling, in which one call returns kcandidates and each candidate is assigned a different framing drawn from a per-pole menu. Procedure.For an item with identifier q and a pole with menuM, we requestk= 6 candidates in a single call. The candidates are returned as a JSON array. The six rewrites restructure the sentence six different ways rather than repeating one edit. The rotation is a deterministic function of q, seeded by an MD5 digest, so runs are reproducible and order-independent. Selection.Candidates are first filtered by the deterministic checks of Appendix E.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Selection.Candidates are first filtered by the deterministic checks of Appendix E. The surviving candidates are then scored by the novelty of their opening words, measured as the number of times that opener has already been kept during the run, and the least-used opener wins. Ties are broken by a per-item seeded permutation of the candidate order, which prevents a fixed menu position from being systematically preferred whenever several candidates score equally. The winning candidate is then passed to the judges. If none passes, the call is repeated, twice for most poles and three times for the charged pole. D.1 System Prompt:indirect You rewrite a user's QUESTION about an email into an INDIRECT, off-record request, changing ONLY its directness — never its meaning. Hard rules: - Preserve the information need EXACTLY: a reader must recover the SAME single answer, and it must be answerable by that same answer. Keep every specific detail (names, dates, numbers, quoted phrases, the subject). Add no new fact and do NOT answer it. - Be genuinely indirect: imply the request via the given mechanism instead of a blunt on-record 'what/who/when'question or command.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Add no new fact and do NOT answer it. - Be genuinely indirect: imply the request via the given mechanism instead of a blunt on-record 'what/who/when'question or command. The output need not be a question. - Stay specific: the reader must still know exactly which detail is asked about. Make it read like a REAL person actually typing this, not an assistant: - First person, natural contractions (I'm, can't, don't, it's, there's). - Plain, concrete, everyday words — NOT formal, elaborate, or corporate vocabulary, and no nominalisations ('clarification is sought'). - Keep it short and a little uneven; a trailing thought or a sentence fragment is fine. - Drop assistant scaffolding: no'I hope this helps','kindly','I would be grateful', no exhaustive hedging, no stiff register. - One clear ask; don't over-explain or pile on qualifiers. 13 Output ONLY the rewritten text: no quotes, labels, or commentary. D.2 Indirectness Mechanisms 1.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: D.2 Indirectness Mechanisms 1. PREPARATORY (hearer's knowledge): imply the ask by wondering whether the reader happens to know or could tell you the specific thing -- not a bare'what/who/when'question. 2. DESIRE (speaker's want): state that you would like or want to know the specific thing, as a wish rather than a question. 3. REASON / MOTIVATION: give the reason or goal that makes the specific answer necessary, and let the request follow from it rather than asking outright. 4. UNMET PRECONDITION: note that you still lack the specific piece of information (you don't have it, or can't find where it is stated), so the need for it is implied. 5. EPISTEMIC UNCERTAINTY: say you can't tell or work the specific answer out from the email, leaving the question implied. 6. ASSOCIATIVE HINT: name the exact detail in the email the answer hangs on and flag that its meaning or reference is unclear, so the reader infers the ask. 7.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: ASSOCIATIVE HINT: name the exact detail in the email the answer hangs on and flag that its meaning or reference is unclear, so the reader infers the ask. 7. UNDERSTATEMENT: be tentative and under-specify -- say you're a little fuzzy or hazy on the specific point, without naming it as a question. 8. PRESUPPOSITION: presuppose the specific answer exists in the email and comment around it rather than requesting it outright. 9. HYPOTHETICAL / CONDITIONAL: embedding the request inside the condition. 10. REPORTED / THIRD-PARTY: frame it as someone else having asked you this and you being unable to answer it from the email. 11. GAP OBSERVATION: point out that the email leaves the specific point unspecified or open, implying you want it resolved. 12. HEDGED APOLOGY: preface with a hedge or apology for possibly missing it, then gesture at the specific point.

D.3 System Prompt:formal You rewrite a user's QUESTION about an email into a formal, professional register — the way a real, competent professional actually writes a courteous work email — changing ONLY the register, never the meaning. Hard rules: - Formal and polite: complete sentences, standard capitalisation and punctuation, no contractions (write'I would','could you', not'I'd','you're') and no slang or abbreviations. - But sound like a REAL PERSON, not an institution. Layer 2: rubric judges.Gate A (Appendix D.15) asks whether the variant requests exactly the same information. Gate B (Appendix D.16) asks whether the variant realizes the target pole, and is given that pole’s fidelity criterion from Appendix D.17. Gate C (Appendix D.18) asks whether the text reads as something a person would genuinely type. All three answer on a single line so the verdict can be parsed deterministically.

Taxonomy.Each generation error carries exactly one code, assigned under a fixed precedence so that no slot is double-counted.E6, not a genuine reader failure, fires first and covers defective gold answers and judge strictness.E3is an answer faithful to one of the other four retrieved emails rather than the gold one.E2bis a real proposition attached to the wrong role, subject or event, andE2aa field filled with a wrong value. These two combines toE2, unsupported content.E4is an answer of the wrong semantic type, for instance a name where a time was asked for.E1is an answer that is not false but incomplete.E5, false abstention, is a claim that the evidence does not contain the answer when it does. Retrieval failures use three codes:R1reports the asked fact absent,R2hedges, andR3 answers confidently anyway. Procedure.Labels were assigned by claude-opus-5.

title: Lost in the Request: How Communication Variation Disrupts Retrieval and Action in Email Agents
text: Procedure.Labels were assigned by claude-opus-5. For each slot it saw the original question, the rewrite, the gold answer with its accepted alternates, the model answer, the baseline answer, and the full text of every retrieved email, and returned one code with a written rationale. One author then reviewed all 118 labels against the same evidence and recoded 23 where the rationale did not support the code under the precedence rule. Slices.An error isstyle-inducedwhen the unperturbed request answered the item correctly and the rewrite broke it (44 slots),persistentwhen the baseline was already wrong ( 65), andbaseline when it is the unperturbed run’s own error (9). Table 8 sets the style-induced slice against the other two pooled, which isolates the kind of failure a rewrite produces. Two codes appear only in the style-induced slice: answering in the wrong semantic type (4 slots) and falsely reporting the answer absent (2), both of which misread the request.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: World models (WMs) simulate the transition dynamics of environments, enabling agents to plan over the consequences of their actions. In text-based environments, fine-tuning a Language Model (LM) to serve as a WM has emerged as a dominant paradigm. However, despite the widespread success of non-parametric approaches such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval for LM-based world modelling remains underexplored. We conduct a systematic evaluation across five diverse environments spanning embodied, web navigation and social settings, comparing fine-tuning and RAG-based approaches for LM-based world modelling. Our study reveals that fine-tuning often outperforms RAG, with fine-tuned WMs enabling agents to obtain higher rewards on 15/20 settings. While both construction paradigms benefit from additional and more diverse exploration, RAG-based approaches prove more data-efficient, and fine-tuning approaches disproportionately benefit from scaling the amount of experience collected. With a focus on RAG-based WMs, we devise a procedure that uses counterfactual intervention to estimate the error rate of the retrieval stage, and show that retrievers consistently surface suboptimal transitions from the experience buffer. Hoping to address this failing, we study a variety of query reformulation strategies, demonstrating that a hierarchical approach outperforms the traditional retrieval pipeline. Finally, we compose our findings into a hybrid world modelling system that parametrically captures core environment dynamics, while learning to rely on retrieval from an actively maintained memory store. Our hybrid system consistently outperforms other methods across multiple environments and models, showcasing the robustness of the approach and the applicability of our findings.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: Agentic systems increasingly improve by scaling experience within complex environments, shifting away from a reliance on dense human annotation and engineered reward systems (Silver & Sutton, 2025). A dominant approach to scaling experience is the development ofworld models (WMs)—internal simulators that learn the underlying transition dynamics of an environment (Ha & ∗Work done during internship at CapitalOne 1 arXiv:2610.02542v1 [cs.AI] 1 Oct 2026 Preprint Schmidhuber, 2018). Using a WM, agents can go beyond simply reacting to the current state and instead plan by considering the consequences of their actions before executing them. To leverage the rich knowledge priors encoded in Language Models (LMs) (Petroni et al., 2019), recent work has explored using LMs as the backbone for world models (Gu et al., 2024). These methods follow the traditional approach to world modelling of collecting exploratory trajectories on a training set, and then finetuning a model to predict future observations (Watter et al., 2015; Chae et al., 2025).

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: These methods follow the traditional approach to world modelling of collecting exploratory trajectories on a training set, and then finetuning a model to predict future observations (Watter et al., 2015; Chae et al., 2025). When applied to LMs, this parametric approach yields WMs that can boost agent performance on a variety of environments, from embodied settings to web-domains (Li et al., 2026). Particularly prominent in the LM domain is the use of non-parametric approaches, such as retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) (Arslan et al., 2024). Relying on the in-context capabilities of LMs, RAG make no changes to the weights, but rather provides examples and additional information relevant to the task at hand to help ground the LM’s response. While both fine-tuning and RAG have their individual strengths (Balaguer et al., 2024), direct comparisons demonstrate that RAG-based approaches can often substantially outperform parametric adaptation in knowledgeacquisition tasks (Ovadia et al., 2024; Soudani et al., 2024).

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: While both fine-tuning and RAG have their individual strengths (Balaguer et al., 2024), direct comparisons demonstrate that RAG-based approaches can often substantially outperform parametric adaptation in knowledgeacquisition tasks (Ovadia et al., 2024; Soudani et al., 2024). However, despite the power of nonparametric approaches, their application to LM-based world modelling remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically compare strategies for constructing LM-based WMs across five environments, including embodied tasks (ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020), TextWorld (Cˆot´e et al., 2018)), web navigation (WebShop (Yao et al., 2022)), and social conversations (Sotopia (Zhou et al., 2024), Chameleon (Karabag et al., 2025)). We construct both fine-tuned and RAG-based WMs and compare their performance on the axes of WM fidelity, as well as agent utility (Section 3.2). Prior studies comparing RAG and fine-tuning frequently find RAG to be dominant in tasks such as knowledge-grounded question answering (Ovadia et al., 2024).

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: Prior studies comparing RAG and fine-tuning frequently find RAG to be dominant in tasks such as knowledge-grounded question answering (Ovadia et al., 2024). Our results show the opposite: RAG underperforms fine-tuning on 15/20 model-environment combinations, but maintains a strong lead on specific environments. Additionally, on 9/20 settings, either fine-tuning or RAG is outperformed by a simple prompting baseline, demonstrating that the ideal approach is highly dependent on the specific environment in question. Ablations over the buffers used to construct the WMs reveal approach-specific trends. Both RAG and fine-tuning benefit from larger and more diverse exploration data; however, RAG is more dataefficient, while fine-tuning exhibits more persistent returns to increases in scale. With a focus on the yet unexplored RAG-based WM approach, we devise a counterfactual intervention experiment to estimate the error rate of the retrieval stage. Our findings are stark and clear: the retrieval step fails consistently with RAG-based WMs, with recall@5 falling below 0.7.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: Our findings are stark and clear: the retrieval step fails consistently with RAG-based WMs, with recall@5 falling below 0.7. Motivated by this finding, we investigate more complex ways of executing retrieval over observations and actions. We find that a hierarchical retrieval paradigm, which selects based on observation similarity before re-ranking based on action similarity, outperforms all other approaches. Finally, we introduce a hybrid paradigm which combines the parametric and RAG-based approaches to construct a world model. Our hybrid approach outperforms every other method on 17/20 modelenvironment combinations, approaching 77% of the utility of an oracle upper bound (compared to 60% by the next best method). On 45% of environment-model combinations, our hybrid exceeds 90% of the performance of the oracle model, establishing the power of the method.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: World Models estimate the transition functionP(s ′|s,a)(Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018). However, since agents are only exposed to observations, world models typically learn a transition function based on observations,P(o′|o,a). World models have a variety of uses, including the replacement of expensive environment calls during agent learning (Hafner et al., 2020), and the enabling of planning over the potential consequences of an agent’s selected actions (Sekar et al., 2020). The traditional approach to training a world model has its roots in image generation (Hafner et al., 2019). First, in the exploration phase, agents collect an experience replay buffer on training splits of the environmentD=   τ (i) N i=1. We then use the transitions from the buffer to train a world model: WM:O×A→Oby minimizing the prediction error:L(θ) =E τ∼D [loss(WMθ(ot,at),ot+1)].

text: We then use the transitions from the buffer to train a world model: WM:O×A→Oby minimizing the prediction error:L(θ) =E τ∼D [loss(WMθ(ot,at),ot+1)]. Since their emergence as powerful aggregators of human knowledge and reasoning skills, there has been increased interest in using LMs to serve as the foundations for WMs (Gu et al., 2024; Chae et al., 2025). These works follow the traditional paradigm, and fine-tune a LM to predict the next observation with a next-token-prediction loss. A strong alternative to finetuning is non-parametric adaptation or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), often used to facilitate memory in agentic systems (Kim & Hwang, 2025; Ferraz et al., 2026). Work on directly using RAG for world modeling has been limited to initial explorations. Prior work (Mei et al., 2025) creates WMs with RAG mechanisms over external, tutorial data to directly reduce the degradation of long-horizon reasoning.
