text: Prior work (Mei et al., 2025) creates WMs with RAG mechanisms over external, tutorial data to directly reduce the degradation of long-horizon reasoning. However, this paradigm requires access to manually curated external datasets, a resource which is hard to gather for many complex environments. To the best of our knowledge, the only work that uses RAG over self collected experience replay buffers to construct LM-based WMs are Yang et al. (2025) and Zhang et al. (2026), however they do not compare against fine-tuning, leaving the comparative strength of the approach unproven. 3 Preprint

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: Prior work in domains such as knowledge acquisition has often directly compared fine-tuning and RAG-based approaches. While neither method is strictly superior to the other (Balaguer et al., 2024), there is widespread agreement that RAG-based approaches enable more effective knowledge acquisition, especially for less popular or domain-specific knowledge (Ovadia et al., 2024; Soudani et al., 2024; Pingua et al., 2025). Existing comparisons of LM-based WMs such as Li et al. (2026), establish a comprehensive evaluation framework for fine-tuned LM-based world models, demonstrating that fine-tuning substantially enhances a LM’s next-state prediction fidelity and long-horizon consistency. However, none of these works consider any RAG-based WMs in their comparisons, leaving open the question of how fine-tuning performs relative to RAG in this domain. Our work addresses this gap and conducts the first systematic comparison of fine-tuning and RAG-based approaches for the task of LM-based world modeling.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: To facilitate a comprehensive evaluation, we compile a diverse testbed of five text-based environments spanning the domains of embodied navigation, web navigation, and social conversations. Embodied Navigation:These environments benchmark embodied decision-making within textsimulated physical spaces. Specifically, we use the ALFWorld and TextWorld environments. In ALFWorld, agents complete household tasks (e.g., “put a clean apple in the fridge”) by navigating rooms and interacting with objects. TextWorld similarly offers procedurally generated text-based quests, such as gathering ingredients to cook a specific recipe. Agents receive a sparse binary reward (+1) upon the successful completion of the high-level task. In these tasks, the WM must learn to predict updated room descriptions, inventory state, or interaction outcomes. Web Navigation:We use the WebShop environment, a simulated e-commerce environment where agents must navigate a web interface to purchase specific items based on natural language instructions (e.g., “buy a red men’s running shoe size 10 under $50”). The agent interacts by issuing search queries and clicking text-based buttons.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: The agent interacts by issuing search queries and clicking text-based buttons. The agent receives a dense scalar reward between 0 and 1 based on the attribute and semantic overlap between the purchased item and the target instruction. The WM must learn to predict search results pages or product details pages. Adversarial Negotiation:To evaluate the agent’s ability to achieve complex social objectives, we simulate two-agent, mixed-motive conversations using scenarios adapted from SOTOPIA. The agent must negotiate effectively against a simulated partner (powered by an LM) endowed with hidden information and competing priorities. For example, the agent may be tasked with securing a $40 loan from a friend who is secretly saving for a major purchase. The agent receives a scalar reward proportional to the resource concessions obtained from the conversation partner by the end of the dialogue. Given the conversation transcript history and the agent’s proposed next utterance, the WM aims to predict the simulated partner’s subsequent conversational response.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: Given the conversation transcript history and the agent’s proposed next utterance, the WM aims to predict the simulated partner’s subsequent conversational response. Deceptive Communication:This environment tests the agent’s capacity for social reasoning and managing implicit information flow via the social deduction game “Chameleon.” In this game, players receive a secret word, except for one player (the Chameleon). Players take turns stating a single related word to prove they know the secret without revealing it to the Chameleon. We simulate a 3-player game where the agent always acts first and is a standard player (non-Chameleon). This reduces to a single-turn decision problem: selecting a word that balances signalling knowledge to peers while obfuscating it from the Chameleon. After every player has stated a word, an external judge guesses which one was the Chameleon.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: After every player has stated a word, an external judge guesses which one was the Chameleon. The agent is rewarded if the Chameleon is correctly accused by the judge, is given zero reward if the other (non-Chameleon) player is accused, and a negative reward if it is accused. Since this is a single-step environment, the WM is trained to predict the subsequent words generated by the other two players, as well as the judge’s verdict, conditioned on the agent’s chosen word. text: We evaluate a range of baseline LM world models. These methods do not require active construction and serve as reference points for the performance of fine-tuned or RAG-based WMs: No WM (No):This setting acts as our foundational, model-free baseline where the agent operates entirely without a world model. Instead of rolling out simulated future states, the agent’s policy directly selects an action based purely on the current observationot. Zero-Shot WM (ZS):We evaluate the inherent, out-of-the-box reasoning capabilities of pre-trained LMs. In this setting, the LM is prompted with the current observationot and actionat, and is tasked with predicting the subsequent stateot+1 relying solely on its pre-trained parametric knowledge. Few-Shot WM (FS):To account for the in-context learning capabilities of modern LMs (Brown, 2020), we augment the prompt withk= 5randomly sampled environmental transitions (oi,ai,oi+1). This evaluates whether standard few-shot demonstration is sufficient to accurately model environment dynamics without the need for targeted retrieval mechanisms.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: We choose a consistent pipeline of deployment for all WMs. All of our experiments involve a frozen, off-the-shelf LM as a policy model/agent (in our study we use Llama3-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Mistral-7B (Jiang et al., 2023), Gemma-4-26B-A4B (Team et al., 2025) and Gemma-4-31B) which uses a world model to plan over its next action. Specifically, the agent sees observationot and instead of predicting a single actiona t, predicts a list of candidate actionsa t,1,...a t,m. The world model under evaluation is used to predict the next observation for each of these candidate actions: ˜o1,...˜om. We then use the policy-agent LM to estimate the value of the predicted observation on a scale of 1-10. The action which led to the most highly rated next observation is selected. In practice, we setm= 5. For exact prompts, hyperparameters and implementation details, see Appendix B.

We follow prior work (Li et al., 2026) and evaluate each WM on two axes: Fidelity:World models predict the next observation. A high-fidelity world model is one that more accurately predicts the next observation. Given that observations can be represented as strings, we use multiple measures of string similarity. Our metrics include lexical overlap (BLEU), semantic overlap (BertScore) and general meaning (Gemma-4-31B-as-a-judge on a scale of 1-10).

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: When evaluating end-to-end task success, fine-tuning is the superior standalone method, achieving superior performance on 15/20 settings. RAG has its strengths; it maintains a consistent advantage over the baseline approaches and outperforms fine-tuning in the Chameleon environment. However, despite the superiority of actively constructed world models, they are not universally optimal. In 9/20 evaluated settings, either FT or RAG is outperformed by non-constructed baselines (No WM, ZS, or FS), reinforcing that the ideal approach remains highly environment-dependent. Interestingly, when isolating the textual accuracy of the predicted next observations, the trend becomes less clear. While FT (4.87) slightly outpaces RAG (4.74) in raw generative accuracy, we notice that in environments such as TextWorld and Sotopia, RAG achieves greater average Fidelity than fine-tuned WMs, despite providing less Utility. This discrepancy correlates with findings from other studies on WMs (Li et al., 2026), which suggest that fidelity, while loosely correlated with total reward, can imply a different ranking over methods. 6 Preprint

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: Since both fine-tuning and RAG-based WMs use replay buffers in their construction, we ask how the nature of the buffer affects the performance of each method. We vary the buffer over two axes: Scale:We subsample the number of points in the buffer to evaluate how performance varies with data scale. Specifically, we construct WMs with experience replay buffers ofntransitions with n∈{10,20,40,80,160,320,640,1280,2560}. Exploration:Previous experiments constructed the buffers using an agent that greedily attempted to solve a task in the training environment. An alternate strategy is to mix exploitation and exploration and have the agent take unguided, exploratory actions in the environmentϵ%of the time. This approach can potentially increase the diversity of states encountered during exploration, enhancing the WM’s effective coverage. In practice, we implement the exploratory action selection mechanism with specialised prompts (see Appendix C) and setϵ∈{0,25,50,75,100}.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: We observe distinct scaling behaviours and exploration preferences between fine-tuning (FT) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) when varying the experience replay buffer. Buffer Scale:Varying the size of the replay buffer reveals contrasting scaling trends. Across TextWorld and Sotopia, RAG achieves strong, near-peak performance with as few asn= 40transitions. However, it tends to plateau or slightly degrade at higher scales. Fine-tuning fails at low scales, yielding near-zero rewards. It consistently reaches an inflexion point aroundn= 80, where performance rapidly accelerates and begins scaling predictably with more data. Exploration Ratio:Injecting exploratory actions during buffer collection improves downstream world model performance, but the optimal distribution diverges by method. For both FT and RAG, completely unguided exploration (ϵ= 100%) and pure exploitation (ϵ= 0%) yield the lowest total rewards across all four environments. Fine-tuning universally peaks atϵ= 75%(e.g., reaching a total reward of 15.04 in TextWorld and 0.88 in Sotopia).

text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) introduces two distinct points of failure: the retrieval mechanism and the generation process. In standard information retrieval, documents can be evaluated against gold-standard annotations. However, transitions in an experience replay buffer lack pre- 7 Preprint Figure 3: Estimated recall of the retriever on Chameleon and TextWorld. Furthermore, a perfectly matching transition may not exist for a given observation-action pair, rendering the quantification of retriever error rates fundamentally ill-posed. To isolate and evaluate the retrieval step, we introduce a pseudo-relevance scoring mechanism. Assume a world model WM(ot,at,e)that predicts the next observation giveno t,at, and a retrieved incontext demonstratione= (o i,ai,oi+1). Let diff(ˆo,ot+1)be an evaluation function (e.g., an LLMas-a-judge) that quantifies the divergence between the predicted observationˆoand the ground-truth observationot+1. By holdingo t andat constant, we counterfactually evaluate candidate transitions from the replay buffer.

text: By holdingo t andat constant, we counterfactually evaluate candidate transitions from the replay buffer. A transitionea is considered strictly better thaneb if: diff(WM(ot,at,ea),ot+1)<diff(WM(o t,at,eb),ot+1)(4) By applying this function, we can empirically assign a pseudo-relevance score to every transition in the buffer, identifying the oracle transition that explicitly minimises the downstream prediction error. In practice, for each test instance,(o t,at), we compute pseudo-relevance scores only for the topk= 20most similar transitions(e 1...e k)ranked by the cosine similarity between the text embedding ofo t◦at ando i◦ai,∀i∈[1,k]. Our metric of interest is Recall@k (k≤5), however we note that since we do not compute pseudo-relevance labels over the entire retrieval corpus, the measures reported below areupper-boundson the recall, i.e., if there is a superior trajectory outside the top-20, it would not affect the recall measure. Evaluating dense retrievers against this oracle reveals severely degraded performance (Figure 3), with upper bounds on Recall@5plateauing at merely70%.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: Evaluating dense retrievers against this oracle reveals severely degraded performance (Figure 3), with upper bounds on Recall@5plateauing at merely70%. This suboptimal recall indicates that offthe-shelf text embedders, trained primarily for semantic similarity, struggle to capture the dynamics of environment transitions. Consequently, there is headroom for optimisation in the retrieval phase. To address these limitations, we investigate alternative query formulations. The naive approach concatenates the observation and action into a single query string. However, this forces semantically distinct modalities into a single representational space, frequently causing one feature to overshadow the other. We propose disentangling the representations through two alternative paradigms: Linear Combination:We independently embed the observation and the action. The final retrieval score is a linear combination of their respective cosine similarities. While this successfully preserves individual modalities, its primary limitation is the reliance on a weighting hyperparameter, which is difficult to tune without a representative validation set. In practice, we weight components equally.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: In practice, we weight components equally. Hierarchical Retrieval:We structure retrieval as a two-stage cascade. First, we retrieve a broad candidate pool (e.g., top-50) based strictly on observation similarity. Second, we re-rank these candidates based on action similarity. This architecture reflects the intuition that the current state is the primary discriminant for environmental context, while the action serves as a secondary filter within similar states, avoiding the retrieval of identical actions in vastly different environments. Results:Evaluating these retrieval paradigms across environments demonstrates that disentangling observation and action representations is generally beneficial, though the method of aggregation is 8 Preprint critical. While a linear combination over independent embedding scores improves performance in WebShop (where it serves as the optimal method) and Chameleon, it actively degrades performance below the simple baseline in TextWorld (4.12) and Sotopia (0.514). Hierarchical retrieval proves more robust. The two-stage cascading approach yields the highest total reward in 3 out of 4 environments (TextWorld, Chameleon, and Sotopia).

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: The two-stage cascading approach yields the highest total reward in 3 out of 4 environments (TextWorld, Chameleon, and Sotopia). The improvement is particularly stark in TextWorld, where it nearly doubles the reward of the naive baseline (12.62 vs. 6.50). This confirms that prioritising observation similarity before filtering by action is an effective, parameter-free heuristic.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: While retrieval provides dynamic context and fine-tuning embeds domain-specific mechanics, both approaches exhibit isolated limitations. To synergise their strengths, we propose a Hybrid World Model (HWM) that integrates supervised fine-tuning with non-parametric retrieval, explicitly training the language model to condition its predictions on retrieved historical experiences. To construct the training pipeline, we populate a transition database with historical episodes. For any given target observation-action pair(ot,at), we utilise a dense vector retrieval mechanism to query the database for semantically similar transitions. However, naive retrieval in sequential environments risks severe data contamination. If left unrestricted, a retriever might simply fetch immediately adjacent frames from the same episode, allowing the model to trivially reconstruct the temporal sequence rather than learning underlying environment dynamics. To prevent this leakage while maximising the utility of the training data, we implement an episodelevel masking filter.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: To prevent this leakage while maximising the utility of the training data, we implement an episodelevel masking filter. If a target transition originates from episodeE i, the retriever is constrained to search exclusively within the disjoint set of all available episodes excludingE i. This strict masking guarantees that the retrieved context acts as a generalised heuristic rather than a direct answer key, preventing intra-episode autocorrelation and ensuring rigorous train-set discipline. The out-of-episode retrieved transitions are then compiled into a structured prompt alongside the targetot andat. We perform supervised fine-tuning on an LM, optimising the standard autoregressive loss on the generation of the ground-truth next observationo t+1.

title: How To Train Your World Model: Fine-tuning vs RAG for LM-based World Modeling
text: In this work, we perform the first systematic comparison of RAG and fine-tuning for the task of LMbased world modelling. We show that unlike tasks like knowledge acquisition, fine-tuning proves consistently superior to RAG, with only minor exceptions. We demonstrate that while both approaches benefit from increased exploration, RAG is more data-efficient. Our error analysis reveals substantial retriever errors, suggesting that adapting the retriever to the specific environment could yield substantial performance gains. We investigate alternative paradigms of encoding transitions and show that a hierarchical scheme outperforms the classic encoding method. Finally, we introduce a hybrid world model system that combines fine-tuning and RAG to consistently outperform all other baselines.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: Campus AI tutors based on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must ground answers in assigned course materials while keeping textbooks and student dialogue on institutional infrastructure. We present CourseChat, an on-premises, multi-course RAG tutor for undergraduate business education, deployed behind a campus web gateway and intended for use embedded in Moodle. Six isolated course offerings, each keyed by its own course reference number (CRN), share twin-edge AI hosts running a FastAPI service, a local vector database, and a local large language model (LLM) served by Ollama. We report two generation-model bake-off rounds, a separate fixed-evidence source-fidelity comparison, and conversation and quiz audits. Several larger models failed the classroom speed gate, but a 12B model and a 7B alternative passed. A separate mixture-of-experts candidate improved some corrections while introducing new factual and continuity errors. We therefore retain the 8B production model pending a demonstrated overall improvement, rather than claiming that 8B is universally optimal. Software changes improved follow-up topic resolution while preserving course scope; 435 prebuilt questions across 65 modules decouple practice from live generation. The results support treating model choice, evidence selection, serving compatibility, and product design as a joint engineering decision. They do not establish learning gains: faculty ratings, peak-load capacity, and complete public-gateway acceptance remain separate evaluation needs.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: Campus AI tutors promise grounded help on assigned materials without sending copyrighted textbooks or student dialogue to external APIs. Realizing that promise under institutional constraints is a systems problem: limited GPU memory, concurrent classroom use, LMS embeds, and a hard requirement that CourseAnever answer from CourseB’s corpus. This paper documents CourseChat, a multi-course RAG tutor deployed for a business school. Students interact through a Moodle-embeddable chat that supports (i) conversation grounded in the selected offering’s indexed materials and (ii) module-scoped practice quizzes with answer keys, hints, and source excerpts. Six offerings (anonymized here as Courses 1–6) share one application binary while remaining isolated at the data and routing layers.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: Six offerings (anonymized here as Courses 1–6) share one application binary while remaining isolated at the data and routing layers. Our central claim is that building such a tutor requires an explicit hardware–software trade-off strategy: choose models and pipelines that fit the host memory and concurrency envelope; push ∗ORCID:https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4193-1154 1 arXiv:2610.02510v1 [cs.AI] 1 Oct 2026 quality into retrieval, scoping, and evaluation rather than into ever-larger generators; and keep product surfaces (conversation vs. quiz) aligned with what the stack can guarantee. The practical question is which component should change when a tutor gives a poor answer. An unhelpful follow-up can originate in lost conversational context, a missing passage, a relevance filter that rejects a useful passage, or a generator that misstates correctly retrieved evidence. A larger model addresses only some of these failures, and its benefits must be weighed against response time and serving compatibility. We use this distinction to organize both the architecture and the evaluation.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: We use this distinction to organize both the architecture and the evaluation. The paper makes three contributions. First, it describes a replicated local RAG architecture and its course-scoping and artifact-management boundaries. Second, it reports a generation-model comparison with fixed retrieval and token limits, alongside a deliberately separate model-andresponse-contract experiment. Third, it connects observed failures to concrete design choices: retrieval-topic resolution, bounded evidence selection, and prebuilt practice banks. Together these provide an evidence-based account of why the current release retains an 8B model despite having enough memory to trial larger ones. CourseChat began as a pilot project at the Dhillon School of Business to explore how a locally developed AI tutor could add value to students’ learning. The university already provides students with access to Copilot and Gemini, and students also use ChatGPT and other generative AI tools. The pilot’s purpose was therefore to complement these existing options with support tailored to local courses, teaching materials, and learning expectations.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: The pilot’s purpose was therefore to complement these existing options with support tailored to local courses, teaching materials, and learning expectations. Rather than replicate general-purpose AI assistance, CourseChat was designed to help students engage with their assigned material and develop the confidence to work independently. Course-grounded explanations, practice questions, hints, and feedback were intended to encourage students to attempt problems themselves, examine their reasoning, and return to the course sources. The intended educational value lay in supporting students’ own effort and understanding, with AI serving as a guide within that process.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: CourseChat brings together three research concerns: how tutoring supports learning, how generated explanations remain faithful to course evidence, and how an institution can serve those interactions reliably. The relevant literature therefore extends beyond comparisons of language-model capability. It also provides reasons to distinguish successful task completion, useful instructional interaction, and learning that persists after assistance is removed. 2.1 Tutoring, practice, and self-regulated learning. Research on intelligent tutoring systems predates conversational language models and emphasizes the organization of instructional support. VanLehn’s review distinguishes systems by the granularity of their interaction, including whether feedback addresses a final answer or intermediate problemsolving steps [2]. Kulik and Fletcher’s meta-analysis of fifty controlled evaluations found generally positive learning effects for intelligent tutoring systems, while also showing that outcomes depend on the comparison condition, assessment, and implementation [ 3]. These findings support studying the instructional process around a response rather than treating fluent dialogue as sufficient evidence of tutoring effectiveness.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: These findings support studying the instructional process around a response rather than treating fluent dialogue as sufficient evidence of tutoring effectiveness. They do not imply that a language-model chatbot inherits the benefits of a validated tutor. Practice and feedback provide a more specific rationale for the pilot’s student controls. In experiments using prose passages, Roediger and Karpicke found that retrieval practice improved 2 delayed retention relative to repeated study, even when restudy produced better immediate performance [4]. The result motivates opportunities to attempt a question before viewing its answer, although it does not establish the effectiveness of CourseChat’s multiple-choice banks. Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick’s account of formative feedback links useful feedback to students’ ability to judge their work and regulate subsequent learning [ 5]. In this framing, a hint or explanation should help a learner identify a gap and decide what to do next.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: In this framing, a hint or explanation should help a learner identify a gap and decide what to do next. CourseChat adopts practice attempts, optional hints, and explanatory feedback as design choices informed by this literature; whether they improve study habits or retention in this setting remains an empirical question.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 2.2 Generative AI assistance and independent learning
text: Recent experiments show why the manner of providing AI assistance matters. Bastani et al. studied generative AI support in high-school mathematics, comparing a relatively unrestricted assistant with a tutor configured to provide teacher-informed instructional support [ 6]. Access to AI improved performance during assisted practice, but students using the relatively unrestricted version subsequently performed worse than the no-AI control group on an unassisted exam. The tutoring safeguards mitigated that reduction; this should not be interpreted as evidence that the guarded condition produced a positive unassisted learning gain. The study distinguishes help with the current exercise from developing the ability to solve another exercise independently. That distinction is directly relevant to a pilot intended to encourage students’ own work rather than merely make answers easier to obtain. Kestin et al. report a complementary result from a randomized crossover study in undergraduate physics: a deliberately designed AI tutor produced higher immediate learning gains than the comparison active-learning class sessions [ 7].

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 2.2 Generative AI assistance and independent learning
text: Kestin et al. report a complementary result from a randomized crossover study in undergraduate physics: a deliberately designed AI tutor produced higher immediate learning gains than the comparison active-learning class sessions [ 7]. The intervention embedded pedagogical guidance and structured content, so it was more specific than access to a general chat interface. Its short instructional scope also limits conclusions about long-term retention, other disciplines, or semesterlong use. Read together, these studies suggest that the instructional design and help policy are part of the intervention being evaluated. They do not support either a universal claim that AI tutoring improves learning or a universal claim that it undermines it. For the Dhillon pilot, this evidence shifts the design question toward the additional educational value of a local service. Students already have other ways to obtain generated text.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 2.2 Generative AI assistance and independent learning
text: Students already have other ways to obtain generated text. CourseChat’s intended contribution is to connect that help to the selected course and give students a practical route between attempting a question, requesting limited assistance, checking an explanation, and returning to the assigned material. This is a rationale for the design, not a claim that the pilot has reproduced either study’s learning outcomes.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: Retrieval-augmented generation provides a technical basis for connecting that help to local materials. Lewis et al. combined a generative model with an external document index, demonstrating improvements on knowledge-intensive tasks and a mechanism for updating accessible evidence separately from model parameters [ 1]. CourseChat uses the broader retrieval-conditioned generation pattern rather than reproducing that paper’s training procedure. Its course collections and module filters determine which teaching materials are eligible to support a response. The resulting benefit is control over the evidence supplied to generation; it does not make the generated answer automatically correct. Gao et al.’s ALCE benchmark evaluates generated answers along separate dimensions of correctness, fluency, and citation quality [ 8]. Their results show that even citation-producing systems can 3 leave claims without adequate support. This distinction matters in education because a valid link to a textbook passage can coexist with an incorrect interpretation of its conditions.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: This distinction matters in education because a valid link to a textbook passage can coexist with an incorrect interpretation of its conditions. CourseChat therefore treats source selection, citation resolution, and fidelity of the explanation as distinct checks. Source cards make evidence inspectable, while answer review must still establish whether the cited passage supports the claim. Increasing the context window is also an incomplete response to grounding failures. Liu et al. found that the position of relevant information affected performance on document question answering and key-value retrieval, with information in the middle of long contexts often used less effectively [ 9]. Their experiments concern particular models and tasks, not the present classroom deployment. Nevertheless, they motivate testing evidence selection and organization instead of assuming that supplying more textbook content will improve an answer. Bounded context, explicit scope, and a fixed retrieval configuration make CourseChat’s model comparisons more interpretable.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: RAG evaluation frameworks reinforce the need to assess components separately. RAGAs proposes reference-free measures for retrieved context, faithfulness, and answer quality [ 10]. ARES uses trained judges to evaluate context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance, together with human annotations to account for judge error [ 11]. These approaches provide useful models for diagnosis, but their scores are not measures of student understanding. CourseChat’s reported evaluation does not claim to implement either framework. It follows the same separation of questions: whether the intended evidence was found, whether the response was supported, and whether the interaction was useful. Faculty assessment and unassisted learning measures address additional questions that automated retrieval or citation checks cannot settle. Serving research also shows why the suitability of a model cannot be inferred from parameter count alone. Kwon et al.’s work on PagedAttention demonstrates that managing the memory used by active generation requests affects batching and throughput [ 12].

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: Kwon et al.’s work on PagedAttention demonstrates that managing the memory used by active generation requests affects batching and throughput [ 12]. Their vLLM results do not predict the performance of CourseChat’s Ollama stack or establish that this deployment would benefit from a particular serving migration. They do establish a relevant systems concern: model weights are only part of the resource demand during concurrent use. CourseChat accordingly treats latency, request overlap, context limits, and client compatibility as evaluation criteria alongside answer quality, while acknowledging that its serial trials do not measure classroom capacity.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: Related course-specific tutors combine retrieval with explicit instructional control. CourseAssist uses course-grounded retrieval, user intent classification, and question decomposition to support computer science students [ 13]. KITE combines multimodal retrieval from course materials with an intent-aware Socratic strategy that provides hints, guiding questions, and progressive scaffolding for algorithmic problem-solving [14]. CourseChat shares their emphasis on course-aligned assistance and develops the operational side of that design: replicated on-premises serving across segregated offerings, model-selection trials under a fixed latency allowance, and prebuilt quiz banks with source bindings and item-review records. Its contribution is evidence about these deployment choices and their observed failure modes in business education. The pilot’s contribution is the integration and evaluation of these concerns within a local businessschool setting. It combines course-specific evidence, conversation continuity, prebuilt practice, and a shared local generator across six separately scoped offerings.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: It combines course-specific evidence, conversation continuity, prebuilt practice, and a shared local generator across six separately scoped offerings. The paper contributes an account of the resulting tradeoffs and failure modes, including why a working 8B configuration was retained 4 despite credible alternatives. It does not propose a new retrieval algorithm, demonstrate superiority over institutionally available AI services, or report a controlled learning-outcome comparison. This position also shapes the next evaluation. A useful local tutor should be assessed for its ability to support appropriate independent effort as well as produce accurate explanations. Measures of unaided problem solving, retention, source use, and patterns of hint requests would connect the engineering results reported here to the educational aims established in the tutoring literature. The present study supplies the implementation and diagnostic evidence needed to design that evaluation.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: 3.1 Student experience. The student experience is organized around the material assigned in a particular course offering. In the intended Moodle integration, students enter through an instructor-provided link embedded in the LMS. CourseChat is meant to sit inside that Moodle course context rather than as a public textbook or tutoring destination: the embed is the intended entry path, and the course slug is not advertised to students as a standalone bookmark, although slug secrecy and enrollment checks are not claimed as proven access controls. That link establishes the full-course, module, or named-activity scope; the header displays the course, instructor, course reference number (CRN), and selected material. This visible context helps students understand which materials the tutor can use and connects the interaction to their immediate coursework. Conversation and quiz functions are implemented in the course pages, while complete acceptance of the public gateway remains a separate deployment task.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: Conversation and quiz functions are implemented in the course pages, while complete acceptance of the public gateway remains a separate deployment task. The design seeks local value through this connection to assigned materials and practice, complementing students’ access to general-purpose AI services. In Conversation mode, students ask questions in ordinary language and receive explanations accompanied by citations to passages from the selected offering. Inline citations open source cards containing excerpts and available chapter, section, or page information. Keeping these cards collapsed initially gives the explanation room while preserving a route back to the original material. Students can request a shorter answer, more detail, or another explanation, and can adjust the explanation level. These controls are intended to support checking and revisiting a concept rather than treating the first generated answer as the endpoint of study.

text: Figure 2 summarizes the campus deployment architecture. The IIS gateway is assigned TLS termination, course-slug rewrites, and routing to two AI nodes (Node A and Node B). title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: We treat model selection as a constrained operating decision. The desired outcome is a useful explanation supported by the selected offering’s materials, delivered within a tolerable classroom wait. The bake-off makes one performance constraint explicit: median complete-answer latency must be no more than 30% above the production 8B baseline measured in the same round. Other promotion criteria require usable overlapping requests, preservation of course scope, and a meaningful improvement in reviewed answers. These are promotion requirements; a listed requirement is not evidence that the corresponding experiment was completed. 7 Several design choices act on different parts of this objective. Model family and size affect answer generation, whereas retrieval depth, context limits, and reranking affect which evidence reaches the model and how soon generation can begin. Server-wide application profiles package these performance settings; they do not select a course or change the collection boundary. A separate product decision moves quiz authoring out of the request path.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: A separate product decision moves quiz authoring out of the request path. A separate deployment decision moves document extraction and review to a workstation, leaving the serving hosts responsible for indexing and inference. Changing these components together would obscure why a candidate succeeded or failed. We therefore keep the serving retrieval stack fixed during the model bake-off, and identify the separate structured-answer experiment as a different comparison. Course content remains local, quiz questions are prepared before practice, and reasoning-capable models must deliver student-visible output within the configured budget before they are considered deployable. These choices trade some flexibility for traceable failures and a bounded release process. Table 1 brings together the main interventions, their observed outcomes, and the resulting design decisions. It distinguishes generator comparisons from changes to retrieval and practice delivery; Section 6 gives the model-by-model measurements. This overview makes explicit why the project retained some components, changed others, and deferred alternatives that had not established an overall advantage.

Each uploaded offering is keyed by its own course reference number (CRN). Instructors can therefore maintain different versions of the same catalog course—for example, distinct sections or successive terms—and control which materials enter that offering’s retrieval collection. Uploading documents updates the evidence available to that CRN; it does not retrain the shared language model or merge corpora across offerings. Two offerings may share a catalog code (e.g., two sections of the same strategic management course) yet must keep distinct corpora when instructors and materials differ.

Passing the reported scope checks supports these specific paths, rather than proving that a shared pretrained model can never produce an unsupported statement.

text: Early demos showed that generating a multiple-choice item at chat time is insufficient for a reliable practice session. The platform therefore prebuilds banks containing source-backed items, keys, explanations, hints, and evidence ledgers. Automatic generation is gated by index and answer evaluation. A separate publication path accepts independently reviewed items bound to the exact current source and question hashes; that path requires the author and reviewer identities to differ, and that item-level review does not clear a failed free-form chat audit. Serving quiz turns is deterministic grading against the bank (warm medians on the order of milliseconds server-local), while conversation retains the generative path. text: Across Courses 1–6 the deployed banks total 435 questions over 65 modules. Structural audits and live API grading checks pass on both nodes; instructor pedagogical review remains an explicit separate gate (instructor reviewed: falseuntil faculty sign-off). This choice makes practice behavior reproducible: the hint, key, explanation, and supporting excerpt can all be inspected before use. It also makes content maintenance explicit. When source material changes, a bank must be checked against the new corpus rather than silently continuing to cite stale evidence. The cost is a finite pool of questions and less spontaneous adaptation to a student’s wording, which is why open-ended explanation remains a separate conversation mode.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 5.4 Conversational turns over shared course evidence
text: Conversation gives students a way to work through the meaning of course material, including questions that cannot be anticipated in a prepared quiz. The design combines three resources with different roles: a pretrained model provides language generation, indexed passages provide current teaching evidence, and prebuilt quiz items provide stable questions, hints, and grading keys. Ingesting a professor’s materials updates the evidence collection; it does not retrain the language model. Conversation can therefore extend the uses of the same corpus while preserving the distinction between an open-ended explanation and a stored practice item. A conversational turn carries more than a new search phrase. If a student asks whether a different assumption would change a worked example, the tutor must retain the example’s setting, identify the changed assumption, and find the course evidence needed to explain its effect.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 5.4 Conversational turns over shared course evidence
text: If a student asks whether a different assumption would change a worked example, the tutor must retain the example’s setting, identify the changed assumption, and find the course evidence needed to explain its effect. An exchange about net present value might move from a definition to a numerical illustration and then to the student’s own account of why a higher discount rate changes the result. This illustrates the intended interaction: the student can test an interpretation and request a targeted explanation. The model’s hypothetical numbers must remain clearly distinguished from facts attributed to course sources, and a change of topic must still respect the selected module. The implemented path resolves dependent turns against recent dialogue while passing the student’s actual wording to generation.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 5.4 Conversational turns over shared course evidence
text: The implemented path resolves dependent turns against recent dialogue while passing the student’s actual wording to generation. Recent dialogue is held in the browser and submitted with each request rather than stored as a durable server session: history must match the selected course, is bounded in length, and does not require sticky affinity between the twin nodes. The shared resolver raised intended-topic follow-up rates to 90–100% across the five-course replay, without changing the generator (Section 8). The conversation router handles social, course, mixed, follow-up, and clarification turns, using deterministic rules first and a short classification call for ambiguity. A casual aside can preserve the course topic; subsequent content questions retrieve fresh evidence. 10 Earlier assistant text helps interpret a reference but is not promoted into authoritative teaching material. Only designated meta or policy FAQ entries short-circuit retrieval; content FAQs remain in the course vector index and compete with other evidence.

text: Only designated meta or policy FAQ entries short-circuit retrieval; content FAQs remain in the course vector index and compete with other evidence. LangChain components already provide model, prompt, document, and vector-store interfaces in the retrieval application. They offer a basis for extending the conversation workflow around the existing corpus: assemble the learning instructions and bounded dialogue, retrieve material for the resolved turn, and generate an explanation with source references. LangChain’s memory facilities support thread-level history and strategies for limiting its size; durable conversation state would additionally require shared persistence and course isolation [ 18]. The current router uses explicit Python control flow and browser-supplied history. A more extensive LangChain workflow, or LangGraph orchestration for resumable multi-step activities, would be a future implementation choice, evaluated against this simpler baseline. This separation creates room for additional instructional modes without building another knowledge base for each one.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor

text: This separation creates room for additional instructional modes without building another knowledge base for each one. A future case-discussion mode could ask students to justify an interpretation using a professor’s supplementary case; a guided-practice mode could focus on the next reasoning step; and a revision mode could revisit a misconception exposed by a quiz. Each would use an explicit interaction policy over the same scoped evidence and keep factual support checks in place. Their local value would come from the instructor’s selected material and teaching expectations, combined with opportunities for student reasoning. These are proposed extensions to the deployed conversation and quiz modes, to be tested for usefulness and appropriate independent effort.

text: 8.1 Multi-turn conversation. Frozen fixtures contain 20 dialogues and 80 turns per course, including 60 follow-ups. They cover numerical examples, misconceptions, topic changes, brevity requests, locked-module boundaries, and transitions between quiz and conversation. The harness records the resolved retrieval query, scope, selected passages, model-visible context, reply, and latency. Topic-hit scores measure whether a dependent question retains its intended subject; they do not measure whether every resulting explanation is correct. Course 1 was evaluated separately, and Courses 2–6 were replayed serially on Node B with the production 8B generator. Table 4 reports the documented before/after topic checks. Course 1 has two live replays; the Courses 2–6 baseline scores come from a resolver-only preflight with the prior production resolver, followed by live evaluation of the update. In the five-course run, all 400 scope checks passed with zero API errors, and each course reached the 90% follow-up target. Median per-turn latency ranged from 3.24 to 6.19 s.

text: Median per-turn latency ranged from 3.24 to 6.19 s. The separate Course 1 replay improved from 31 to 60 successful follow-ups, while its median increased from 4.92 to 5.81 s. This is consistent with treating quality and speed as distinct outcomes rather than assuming that every resolver improvement also reduces latency. The five-course run still contained 93 no match turns. Twelve were intentional locked-module refusals, fifteen were quiz follow-ups whose wording did not retrieve a qualifying passage, and 66 involved other requests spanning 24 topics. Cleaner concept probes found evidence for nineteen of those topics; five still required content or index investigation. A bounded facet expansion recovered eleven of the 24 original questions without lowering the relevance floor. These diagnostics identify recoverable retrieval failures; they are not an overall answer-accuracy score. Faculty ratings remain pending, so neither the proposed 4/5 usefulness target nor the 95% supported-claim target is claimed as achieved. 15

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: A targeted, agent-reviewed ten-request live textbook audit gives a complementary view of quality. It found three supported replies, four retrieval misses despite available evidence, two source contradictions, and one partly grounded answer. Every returned citation resolved to its source. Thus, citation integrity coexisted with substantive error: locating a real passage did not ensure that the answer preserved its meaning. The requests were selected diagnostics, not a representative sample from which to estimate a population error rate. The 20 September router extension has a different evaluation scope. Its frozen contract contains 32 crossover cases, supplemented by focused checks and live probes for social, mixed, course, followup, and ambiguous turns. Both nodes passed 306 focused Python tests and the documented live probes before activation. This supports the routing implementation; it does not retroactively turn the earlier conversation runs into tests of that extension, or establish faculty-rated usefulness.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: Both nodes passed full artifact and grading audits for all 65 modules. The artifact audit bound each question to its current source excerpt and original file hashes, then exercised all 435 questions, including deliberately wrong answers. It checked that hints do not reveal keys or advance progress, and that requests cannot carry another course’s quiz state into the selected offering. These checks establish reproducible practice behavior. A separate 166-request live API audit included all 65 module starts on each node, plus warm repeats, hints, and graded answers. Warm medians were 4.8 ms on Node A and 5.8 ms on Node B, measured server-local. They describe stored quiz operations and must not be compared as if they were generative tutoring latencies or browser response times. Instructor review of answer correctness, distractors, difficulty, and instructional coverage remains incomplete.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: 9.1 Why retain the 8B classroom generator?. Retaining llama3.1:8b is a deployment decision under incomplete quality evidence, rather than a claim that eight billion parameters is an optimal model size. The first bake-off established that several plausible upgrades increased full-answer latency substantially under the same retrieval and output budget. The second round qualified that result: Qwen 7B ran at almost the baseline speed, and Mistral Nemo 12B stayed inside the prescribed 30% latency allowance. Consequently, “larger models are too slow” does not adequately explain the final choice. The production policy requires a clear grounded-tutoring benefit in addition to acceptable speed. Passing twelve keyword-and-citation checks, or producing slightly more complete answers on that set, does not establish that benefit. The documented decision is to keep the existing generator while faculty compare the alternatives on the quality of their actual explanations. This choice preserves a known serving configuration while acknowledging its material weaknesses.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: This choice preserves a known serving configuration while acknowledging its material weaknesses. The fidelity diagnostic reproduced incorrect accounting claims, failure to correct an earlier pricing error, and attribution of an equation to an exercise that did not state it. Those failures preclude treating continued deployment as evidence that the 8B model has passed the proposed claim-support target. The defensible rationale is narrower: no evaluated replacement has yet demonstrated the complete combination of quality, continuity, integration, and operational readiness required for promotion. A reviewed Qwen 7B or Nemo 12B improvement could change that decision without changing the architecture. 16

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.2 A model is evaluated through its serving contract
text: The separate structured-response experiment illustrates why parameter count alone is a poor predictor of either speed or usefulness. With thinking disabled, the 35B-A3B mixture-of-experts candidate had a lower warm median than the 8B baseline on the twelve fixed-source cases. It corrected important misconceptions that persisted in the baseline, but also overstated the protection provided by holding cash and refused an answerable reference to a previous example. These are consequential tutoring regressions: a student needs an explanation to preserve both the source’s conditions and the setting established in the conversation. That comparison held the evidence and dialogue fixed but changed the model, prompt, output schema, validation, and transport together. Its gains therefore belong to the complete candidate configuration; they cannot be attributed solely to model scale. Conversely, an empty response in the original production-client bake-off does not show that the underlying model lacks knowledge.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.2 A model is evaluated through its serving contract
text: Conversely, an empty response in the original production-client bake-off does not show that the underlying model lacks knowledge. The installed serving stack did not consistently apply the structured format to thinking-capable chat requests when thinking was disabled. A direct generation request resolved the observed JSON-formatting problem, while factual and continuity failures remained. Runtime compatibility thus belongs in the experimental specification alongside model tag, quantization, context length, and sampling options. The experimental answer contract also left production streaming and instructor-specific instructions uncertified, providing another reason to withhold activation.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.3 Grounding requires useful answers and appropriate abstention
text: The evidence suggests that stricter output validation trades some unsupported answers for refusals, without eliminating semantic error. In the final candidate, all twelve outputs were valid JSON and nine passed the quotation and citation checks. An accepted answer nevertheless strengthened a conditional financial benefit into a guarantee. Of the three withheld answers, two lacked sufficient evidence and one was an answerable follow-up. Exact quotation verifies a textual relationship with a source; it does not verify that the explanation preserves the source’s meaning. The separate entailment experiment reinforces this distinction. Its proposed contradiction threshold missed both original production errors, even though the classifier detected simplified versions of some errors. A hypothetical teaching example also received a neutral label, showing why rejecting all non-entailed prose would suppress legitimate instruction. A useful tutor must distinguish course-supported concepts, explicitly invented example values, unavailable facts, and unjustified real-world guarantees. Evaluation should therefore report unnecessary abstention and loss of explanatory context alongside unsupported claims. Evaluation should therefore report unnecessary abstention and loss of explanatory context alongside unsupported claims. The proposed bounded revision experiment addresses these failure modes, but it remains future work; neither a runtime factual guard nor a reliable semantic repair mechanism has been demonstrated.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.4 Retrieval and conversation control are complementary to generation
text: The multi-course resolver results identify a substantial source of improvement outside the generator. Resolving a short follow-up into its intended retrieval topic allows the existing model to receive relevant teaching material while still answering the student’s actual wording. Course and module boundaries remain enforceable in this step. However, a correct topic does not ensure that an adequate passage will be retrieved, and an adequate passage does not ensure that the model will explain it faithfully. The five-course audit’s remaining retrieval misses, and the fixed-evidence fidelity failures, demonstrate these distinct failure layers. This decomposition helps allocate engineering effort. Clean-concept probes recovered evidence for nineteen of twenty-four affected topics, indicating that many misses arose from query formula- 17 tion. Five topics still failed under that favorable probe and required corpus, index, or threshold investigation. A bounded expansion using only words in the student question recovered eleven of the original queries without lowering the relevance floor.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.4 Retrieval and conversation control are complementary to generation
text: A bounded expansion using only words in the student question recovered eleven of the original queries without lowering the relevance floor. These findings support targeted retrieval work; they do not imply that query processing can repair missing material or generation errors. Preserving each turn’s resolved query, selected passages, and displayed answer makes that distinction auditable and reduces the temptation to attribute every poor answer to model size. The subsequent conversation router, activated on both nodes on 20 September, extends this separation to social, course, mixed, follow-up, and clarification turns. Obvious cases use deterministic rules; ambiguous cases use a short structured classification request to the same 8B model. Sharing the resident model avoids introducing a second model and a possible model-loading penalty while routing is evaluated. Its validated intent schema is a deployed control mechanism, distinct from the experimental evidence-first answer contract discussed above.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.4 Retrieval and conversation control are complementary to generation
text: Its validated intent schema is a deployed control mechanism, distinct from the experimental evidence-first answer contract discussed above. The implementation also illustrates a deliberate complexity trade-off: bounded browser-supplied history and a small Python router meet the current requirements, while durable cross-device conversations would require additional persistence. LangGraph remains an option for that future requirement, rather than a dependency needed to obtain the reported improvements.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: Local inference and separate offering collections give the institution control over where course materials and student dialogue are processed and which evidence enters an answer. Dialogue is handled on the campus hosts rather than sent to an external generation API. Each offering is keyed by its own CRN, so instructors can maintain different versions of the same catalog course and decide which materials that version may retrieve. Sharing one generator across offerings avoids maintaining six content-specific language models, while separate collections, data trees, browser-held histories, and request routing keep those CRN boundaries in place. Uploaded materials update the retrieval collection for the selected offering; they are not used to fine-tune a shared model on faculty or student content. Access is organized around the LMS course context and course routing rather than an application- level enrollment check in CourseChat itself. These mechanisms support reproducible content updates and instructor-controlled corpora.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: These mechanisms support reproducible content updates and instructor-controlled corpora. Their evaluation demonstrates scoped behavior on the recorded probes, rather than a general proof of security, privacy compliance, or enrollment enforcement. The two complete local stacks provide an operational alternative when one node is under maintenance, but duplicate state introduces explicit maintenance work. Updating the primary index is insufficient: the replica must receive the corresponding snapshots, and quiz banks and evidence ledgers must be copied separately. Code, model configuration, and course artifacts also need consistent versions. This is the cost of retaining local ownership and independently serviceable hosts. The reported work does not measure capital amortization, electricity, administration time, or cost per student; it therefore supports no claim that this deployment is cheaper than a cloud service. Its demonstrated motivation is control under the institution’s chosen deployment constraints.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.6 Prebuilt practice moves uncertainty into a reviewable build stage
text: Prebuilding quizzes changes both the computational and educational trade-off. Serving a stored question and grading against its key avoids a generation request for each practice turn, while making hints and explanations stable across sessions. It also makes evidence and arithmetic review possible before an item reaches a student. In exchange, the bank offers finite variation and requires rebuilding or re-review when course material changes. Six or seven questions per module establish availability 18 across the module map, rather than exhaustive coverage of each learning objective. The distinction between artifact integrity and teaching quality remains essential. Successful grading and exact source bindings demonstrate that practice behaves consistently, but they cannot establish suitable difficulty, plausible distractors, or a single pedagogically defensible answer. All banks still record instructor review as incomplete. Similarly, a module with limited source material can offer bounded, supported practice without claiming comprehensive coverage. This explicit limitation is preferable to letting live generation silently supply missing instructional content.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.7 Faculty review, student uptake, and educational value
text: The next pilot stage should connect content maintenance to teaching practice. Instructors could identify recurring misconceptions, contribute supplementary cases or worked examples, and review the questions generated from those materials. A useful approval workflow would present each question alongside its answer, distractors, hint, explanation, and supporting excerpts, allowing the instructor to edit, approve, or return it for revision. The existing source bindings and itemreview records provide an artifact foundation for this workflow; a streamlined faculty interface and completed instructor approval remain future work. Preserving approved edits and requesting renewed review when their supporting material changes would make this feedback loop part of maintaining a course, rather than a one-time inspection of generated content. Student uptake should be evaluated over a teaching period. Initial visits would show reach, while return visits and continued use across later modules would help distinguish sustained use from novelty. Reporting use separately for explanation, conversational follow-up, and quiz practice would reveal which activities students find valuable.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.7 Faculty review, student uptake, and educational value
text: Reporting use separately for explanation, conversational follow-up, and quiz practice would reveal which activities students find valuable. Course coverage also matters: a service used intensively in one offering may fit that instructor’s materials without transferring to other courses. These observations should be paired with student feedback on usefulness, ease of use, trust in source-supported answers, and reasons for abandoning an interaction. Acceptance cannot be inferred from usage counts alone, particularly where an instructor explicitly encourages participation. Educational evaluation should examine what students can do after assistance. A future study could combine interaction measures, such as attempts before revealing answers and responses to hints, with delayed assessments and new problems completed without the tutor. Appropriate comparisons include the existing course resources and the general-purpose AI tools students already use. Comparing equivalent learning tasks would help establish whether access to instructor-selected evidence and reviewed practice adds value beyond convenient text generation.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.7 Faculty review, student uptake, and educational value
text: Comparing equivalent learning tasks would help establish whether access to instructor-selected evidence and reviewed practice adds value beyond convenient text generation. Perceived usefulness, assisted task performance, and independent learning should remain separate outcomes. Faculty acceptance is equally consequential. The pilot should record the time needed to prepare materials, review questions, resolve reported errors, and update a course between offerings. A proposed feedback mechanism could let students flag an unclear explanation or disputed answer for instructor review, with confirmed issues feeding into corpus corrections and regression cases. This would connect observed difficulties to concrete revisions while making the teaching workload visible. Together, student and faculty evidence would guide which interaction modes to extend and which content gaps deserve attention first.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.8 Limits of the evidence and next evaluation priorities
text: The reported latency measurements are predominantly serial and server-local. Two API workers permit overlapping requests, but worker count and available memory do not establish usable classroom throughput. Warm model timings also exclude the substantial cold-load delay observed for the larger candidate. The two-request overlap gate remains a requirement for promotion; the 19 presented results do not constitute a completed load study. Gateway time-to-first-token requires separate measurement because proxy buffering can delay visible output without changing generation time. SSE support is implemented, whereas public gateway readiness and verification for every course slug remained open in the documented deployment snapshot. The evaluation sets are engineering regressions rather than a representative sample of student use. Repeated development on frozen fixtures can improve those cases without transferring to unseen misconceptions or question forms. Faculty ratings for usefulness and factual support remain pending, and no learning-outcome or controlled classroom study is reported.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
section: 9.8 Limits of the evidence and next evaluation priorities
text: Faculty ratings for usefulness and factual support remain pending, and no learning-outcome or controlled classroom study is reported. The next evidence needed is therefore paired faculty review on held-out dialogues, explicit measurement of false refusals and source-condition errors, and concurrent browser-to-gateway timing under representative load. These checks would make a future model change defensible while preserving the current distinction between an implemented system, measured engineering behavior, and demonstrated educational benefit.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: CourseChat began as a Dhillon School of Business pilot to provide useful local learning support alongside the generative AI services already available to students. Its contribution rests on the design of the whole teaching system: separate CRN-scoped collections preserve instructional context and let instructors control which materials each offering may retrieve, a traceable ingestion pipeline connects responses to supplied materials, conversation controls support follow-up questions, and prebuilt quizzes make practice and feedback inspectable. These choices allow one shared generator to serve different offerings while giving course content and instructional interaction their own development and review processes. They also expose practical trade-offs, including preparation effort, finite question-bank variety, and the need to keep replicated course artifacts consistent. The model trials inform one part of this design. We retain llama3.1:8b because the evaluated alternatives have not yet demonstrated an overall advantage across grounded explanation, conversational continuity, latency, and serving compatibility. Credible 7B and 12B candidates remain available for further assessment.

title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware-Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
text: Credible 7B and 12B candidates remain available for further assessment. The choice is therefore conditional on evidence and can change without rebuilding the course architecture. The observed retrieval and fidelity failures also show why improving a tutor requires attention to evidence preparation and dialogue handling alongside model capability. The next development stage should extend the course ingestion pipeline with relevant, reviewed material supplied by instructors: supplementary cases, worked examples, lecture explanations, and contextual material beyond the core assigned text. Better coverage can address missing evidence, but adding documents alone does not ensure better answers; extraction quality, module mapping, retrieval, and explanation fidelity must be evaluated together. A shared, versioned corpus can support several interaction modes, including course discussion, guided examples, concept comparison, and quiz practice, without maintaining a separate knowledge base for each mode. These modes would complement general-purpose assistants such as ChatGPT by centering the instructor’s selected context, expectations, and review of teaching materials.

The local service’s purpose is to help students reason within that context and apply it themselves. Faculty participation should shape that development. A review workflow can allow professors to inspect, revise, and approve quiz items and their supporting evidence, while student reports of unclear or incorrect explanations can inform subsequent content and evaluation updates. Existing review artifacts provide a starting point; instructor approval of the current banks is still pending. The next pilot should assess sustained student uptake, acceptance of different interaction modes, and the 20 workload this process creates for faculty. Delayed and unassisted assessments, alongside comparisons with existing resources and general-purpose assistants, would establish whether the system supports independent learning. These findings should guide its expansion toward an instructor-informed learning environment whose value comes from local context, useful feedback, and students’ own effort.

title: Mapping the RAG Landscape: A Four Axis Taxonomy of Efficiency, Defense, Interactivity, and Reasoning
text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable fluency across many tasks but remain limited by their static, parameter bound knowledge and their susceptibility to hallucinating information. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these issues by incorporating external retrieval into the generation process, grounding model outputs in verifiable and up to date sources. While prior surveys primarily focus on core RAG architectures and standard pipelines, recent research explores broader challenges and capabilities that extend beyond these foundational designs. This survey provides a consolidated and structured examination of contemporary RAG developments, organizing the field into a four axis taxonomy: improving retrieval efficiency, strengthening robustness and security, supporting user driven and interactive workflows, and enabling multi step or complex reasoning. We formalize key components of the RAG framework and review methods spanning dense and sparse retrieval, fusion strategies, embedding optimizations, and reinforcement learning based retrieval policies, highlighting how these advances influence practical deployment and system design. We also synthesize evaluation practices, domain specific applications, and architectural variants such as Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG. Finally, we outline persistent challenges related to retrieval quality, reliability, domain adaptation, scalability, and explainability, and identify opportunities for building RAG systems that are more reliable, adaptable, and transparent.
