title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: For each levellof the DAG, the candidate nodes are ranked by a function Sl(·), which combines contributions from the original queryqand the cumulative queryq c. In order to defineS l(·), we first introduce the level-aware similarity function as follows: Sim(s,ei,l) = cos(e s|ml,ei)(3.2) Here,sis a text,e s is its embedding, andes|ml is them l-length prefix ofe s. The second argument of the function is the embeddingei stored at the levellof the DAG. Iflis an internal level, thenei is the embedding of a centroid atl; instead, iflis a leaf, thene i is the embedding of a document inD. In both cases,e i is already stored as anml-length vector, so it does not require truncation. The similarity functionS l(·)returns a score that combines two contributions. The first contribution is the similarity ofei to the original queryq, which anchors the search to the original information need [27].

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: The first contribution is the similarity ofei to the original queryq, which anchors the search to the original information need [27]. The second contribution is the similarity ofei to the cumulative queryq c, which expandsqwith the content of the documents retrieved thus far via PRF [46]: Sl(ei) =β t·Sim(q,e i,l) + (1−β t)·Sim(q c,ei,l)(3.3) where the anchoring coefficientβt is defined as follows: 11 βt =|Rt−1| K (3.4) Inthefirstiteration,q c =qandβ t = 0, whichreducesSl(ei)toSim(q,e i,l). As documents are collected,qc incorporates their content progressively and may drift away from the original information need. Concurrently,β t increases, shifting the weight towardqand preventing semantic drift. The traversal begins at the coarsest level (i.e.,l= 1) and continues downward. At each levell, we apply the functionS l(·)to each centroid atl. Then, we select the centroide x oflwith the highest value ofS l(·). Afterwards, we restrict the candidate set to the nodes at the levell+ 1 that are connected to the node corresponding toex.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: Afterwards, we restrict the candidate set to the nodes at the levell+ 1 that are connected to the node corresponding toex. Due to thep-nearest assignment introduced in Section 3.1, each node at the levell+ 1can be reached from up topnodes at the levell. Thus, the traversal can tolerate suboptimal centroid choices without losing relevant candidates. We repeat this process until the levelLis reached. At this level, the candidates are documents inD, and their embeddings are stored at the full dimensionM. Since each levell<Loperates at a lower dimensionm l <M rather than the full dimensionM, and since the candidate set is progressively restricted as the traversal proceeds, the similarity computations at the coarser levels are cheaper and performed over a smaller set of candidates. This reduces the overall cost compared to a flat search over the full corpus at the dimensionM.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: After traversing to the levelL, we re-rank the candidates using the set of newentitiesB t−1 (seeSection3.2). Tothisend, weusetheJaccardcoefficient to measure the overlap between the set of entitiesEi of a candidate document di and the set of new entitiesBt−1 as follows: J(di) =|Bt−1∩Ei| |Bt−1∪Ei| (3.5) The final scoreR(di)of a documentd i at the levelLcombines semantic similarity and entity overlap as follows: R(di) =α·S L(ei) + (1−α)·J(d i)(3.6) whereαcontrolstherelativeimportanceoftheentitysignal. TheJaccard coefficient ranges in the real interval[0,1]and is therefore stable with respect to the scale of cosine similarity. TheRetrievefunction returns the top 12 documents, ranked byR(di), within the budgetKdefined in Section 3.2. These documents form the setDt and are then accumulated intoRt by the retrieval loop.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: This section presents an experimental evaluation of MatRAG. Specifically, Subsection 4.1 describes the experimental setup. Subsection 4.2 examines the impact of the main hyperparameters. Subsection 4.3 reports the main results. Finally, Subsection 4.4 presents an ablation study that evaluates the contribution of each component of MatRAG. 4.1 Experimental Setup. In this section, we describe the setup used during our experimental campaign. Specifically, we focus on the datasets used, the baselines selected for comparison, some implementation choices for MatRAG, and the evaluation metrics.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: We evaluated MatRAG on three standard multi-hop QA benchmarks, namely HotpotQA [40], 2WikiMultiHopQA (2Wiki) [10], and MuSiQue [36]. Each dataset requires aggregating evidence from multiple documents to answer a question, though datasets differed in the type of reasoning involved. In fact, HotpotQA covers bridge and comparison questions, 2Wiki focuses on compositional reasoning over Wikipedia, and MuSiQue is designed to resist shortcut-based retrieval. All three benchmarks provide gold answers, i.e., reference strings against which generated answers are evaluated. The benchmarks also provide gold supporting documents, which are subsets of the corpus documents containing the evidence necessary to answer each question. We used these documents to compute retrieval metrics. The document corpora contain9,811documents for HotpotQA,6,119 documents for 2Wiki, and11,656documents for MuSiQue. While previous studies typically relied on a single sample of1,000questions [7, 25], we drew five independent samples of1,000questions each to reduce variability in question selection.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: While previous studies typically relied on a single sample of1,000questions [7, 25], we drew five independent samples of1,000questions each to reduce variability in question selection. We evaluated all methods on the same five samples, and we report the mean and standard deviation of each metric across them. We selected hyperparameter values using a separate validation set of 500 questions per benchmark that was disjoint from the test split. 13

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: WecomparedMatRAGwithsevenrepresentativeRAGsystemsthatspan the main families of approaches discussed in Section 2. As a reference for flat retrieval, we included NaiveRAG, which performs dense retrieval over a FAISS1 flat index. As a representative of the hierarchical family, we included RAPTOR [30]. The remaining baselines covered graph-based and reasoning-augmented approaches; they are: GraphRAG [4], LightRAG [6], HippoRAG2 [8], KGP [39], and ToG [32]. For all baselines, we followed the original implementations and adopted the hyperparameter settings reported in the papers introducing them. To ensure a fair comparison, all baselines used the same generative model (gemma3:27b-it-qat2 via Ollama) for answer generation.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: All systems that require dense retrieval, including MatRAG, use the nomic-embed-text-v1.5 [20] as the embedding model. This model natively supports MRL at the following dimensions:{64,128,256,512,768}. We adopted it as the Matryoshka dimension schedule for MatRAG, settingL= 5 andM= 768. We stored the five levels of the DAG at the corresponding dimensions. Documents at the leaves maintained the full dimensionM= 768, while internal clusters used progressively shorter prefixes toward the coarsest level, which was stored atm1 = 64. We selected the values of the total retrieval budgetK, the similarity weightα, and the DAG overlapping factor pvia the hyperparameter analysis reported in Section 4.2. In particular, based on this analysis, we setK= 10,p= 2, andα= 0.5consistently across all datasets. We conducted all experiments on a server equipped with an NVIDIA A100 GPU (40 GB VRAM) and 128 GB of system RAM. The interested reader can find the implementation code at the following link: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MatRAG.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: We evaluated the quality of the answers using Exact Match (EM) and token-level F1, computed against the gold answers [40, 10, 36]. To measure retrieval quality independently of the generative step, as in previous studies [8, 7], we employed Recall@2 (R@2) and Recall@5 (R@5). For each question, R@2 (resp., R@5) measures the number of gold supporting documents found among the top two (resp., five) retrieved documents divided by 1https://faiss.ai/cpp_api/struct/structfaiss_1_1IndexFlatIP.html 2https://ollama.com/library/gemma3:27b-it-qat 14 the total number of gold supporting documents for that question. We averaged these values across all questions in a dataset. We only computed these retrieval metrics for MatRAG, HippoRAG2, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG, as these approaches retrieve documents directly from the corpus. The remaining baselines retrieve units not directly comparable to corpus documents. These include the node summaries of RAPTOR, the community summaries of GraphRAG, the passages of KGP (which have a different level of detail than the gold supporting documents), and the KG entities and relationships of ToG.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: These include the node summaries of RAPTOR, the community summaries of GraphRAG, the passages of KGP (which have a different level of detail than the gold supporting documents), and the KG entities and relationships of ToG. For these systems, the gold document overlap required by R@2 and R@5 was undefined. In addition to assessing retrieval and answer quality, we evaluated the efficiency of each system based on indexing time (Idx), response time (Res), andLLMcontextsize(Tok). Indexingtimeistheamountoftime, inseconds, required to build the index from the corpus. Response time is the average time, in seconds, for each retrieval and answer generation. LLM context size is the average number of tokens passed to the generative model per question.

text: In this section, we describe the analyses we performed to tune the hyperparameter values. To avoid tuning on the test data, we ran our analyses on a separate validation set of 500 questions for each dataset. We sampled this set disjointedly from the questions used for the test data (see Section 4.1). All reported values are means over this validation set. First, we evaluated the effect of the retrieval budgetKby considering two values of this parameter:K= 5andK= 10. The results are reported in Table 1. In each column of this and the following tables, the optimal value is in bold, and the suboptimal value is underlined. An upward-pointing (resp., downward-pointing) arrow next to a metric indicates that its optimal value is the highest (resp., lowest). The analysis of this table shows that increasing Kfrom 5 to 10 substantially improves the EM and F1 scores across all datasets.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering

As for EM, there are gains of 16.34% on HotpotQA, 19.25% on 2Wiki and 21.36% on MuSiQue. Regarding F1, we observe improvements of 8.56% on HotpotQA, 19.34% on 2Wiki and 21.45% on MuSiQue. Conversely, we observe an increase in Tok, which increased by 108.00% on HotpotQA, 104.03% on 2Wiki, and 102.26% on MuSiQue. text: In this section, we assess the two core components of MatRAG (i.e., the anchoring strategy and the Matryoshka indexing scheme) by comparing them with simpler alternatives. Unlike the hyperparameter analysis, which was performed on the validation set to avoid tuning on test data, this ablation study does not involve hyperparameter selection. Therefore, we employed the same test samples used in Section 4.3 to ensure comparability with the main results. We started by analyzing the effect of the query anchoring strategy, controlled byβt. Specifically, we considered three alternatives, namely:(i)using only the original query (q);(ii)using only the cumulative expanded query (qc); and(iii)using an adaptive combination of the two. The results are reported in Table 8. This table shows that relying exclusively on either signal is suboptimal. Using only the original query (βt = 1.00) limits the ability to incorporate newly discovered contexts, thereby undermining multi-hop performance.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: Using only the original query (βt = 1.00) limits the ability to incorporate newly discovered contexts, thereby undermining multi-hop performance. Conversely, using only the expanded query (βt = 0.00) introduces semantic drift because irrelevant information may accumulate across iterations. The formulation proposed in MatRAG (see Equation 3.4) balances these two contributions dynamically by gradually increasing the weight of the original query to maintain alignment with the initial information need. It achieves the optimal trade-off across all datasets and metrics. For instance, it increases F1 by1.95%compared to the base variant (βt = 1.00) on HotpotQA and by11.34%on 2Wiki. It also improves F1 by4.75%over the expanded-query variant (βt = 0.00) on MuSiQue. These results highlight the importance of managing query drift in iterative retrieval and show that the proposedβt scheduling provides a consistent and effective scoring mechanism for different levels of reasoning complexity.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: One of the core hypotheses of MatRAG is that the semantic hierarchy of a clustering structure can be exploited through the nested MRL structure. This means that coarser levels can be indexed at shorter prefix dimensions without a significant loss of discriminative power. The retrieval results support this hypothesis; in fact, MatRAG outperforms the baselines on most metrics while operating with a lower dimensionality of the embeddings at the upper levels of the DAG. The largest improvements are seen in MuSiQue, which may suggest that hierarchical traversal is most beneficial when singledocument similarity is insufficient to identify the relevant evidence chain. Another core component of MatRAG is the entity-Jaccard re-ranking signal. Hyperparameter analysis (Table 3) shows that the entity score complements semantic similarity. Removing it entirely (α= 1.00) reduces performance, particularly on 2Wiki, where compositional reasoning chains tend to introduce numerous named entities across hops.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: Removing it entirely (α= 1.00) reduces performance, particularly on 2Wiki, where compositional reasoning chains tend to introduce numerous named entities across hops. Conversely, relying exclusively on the entity signal (α= 0.00) also results in poor performance, as entity overlap alone cannot capture semantic relevance. The optimal balance is achieved atα= 0.50across all datasets, indicating that the two signals complement each other. Furthermore, the adaptive anchoring schedule shows that neither anchoring the search exclusively to the original query nor expanding it without control is sufficient. This is because the interpolation guided byβt is necessary to exploit the retrieved context and, at the same time, prevent semantic drift. This tension cannot be solved by static scoring strategies. The clustering analysis provided further evidence in support of the central hypothesis of MatRAG. As shown in Table 9, the clusters obtained from truncated Matryoshka prefixes are competitive with those obtained from full-dimensional embeddings and tend to produce slightly better clustering 24 quality.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: As shown in Table 9, the clusters obtained from truncated Matryoshka prefixes are competitive with those obtained from full-dimensional embeddings and tend to produce slightly better clustering 24 quality. This is refelected in lower DB indices and higher Silhouette scores in several configurations. This suggests that, at the coarser levels of the hierarchy, the additional dimensions of the full embedding contain redundant information for forming well-separated clusters, which is removed by truncation. Consequently, the Matryoshka indexing scheme reduces the cost of similarity computations without compromising the quality of the hierarchy. After verifying that MRL maintains the quality of the hierarchy, a complementary question is whether this also applies to end-to-end retrieval, in which truncated representations are used to traverse the DAG and rank documents. Tables10and11addressthisissuebycomparingMatryoshka’struncated and full-dimensional embeddings during retrieval. Across all benchmarks, the Matryoshka configuration achieves better performance consistently in terms of both QA metrics and retrieval recall while reducing response time.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: Across all benchmarks, the Matryoshka configuration achieves better performance consistently in terms of both QA metrics and retrieval recall while reducing response time. These results suggest that truncating embeddings to a lowerdimensional subspace, as enabled by MRL, does not degrade retrieval quality. This behavior can be attributed to the way Matryoshka embeddings are trained, as the most semantically relevant information is encoded in the leading dimensions. This effectively concentrates the signal and reduces noise in the higher-dimensional components. Consequently, using only the truncated embedding prefixes acts as a form of implicit regularization, as it discards dimensions that provide little discriminative information and could introduce spurious similarity signals. The observed efficiency gains in response time further reinforce the practical appeal of this design choice, as operating on lower-dimensional vectors makes the retrieval step computationally cheaper without sacrificing the quality of the retrieved documents or the downstream answers.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: The observed efficiency gains in response time further reinforce the practical appeal of this design choice, as operating on lower-dimensional vectors makes the retrieval step computationally cheaper without sacrificing the quality of the retrieved documents or the downstream answers. The results obtained in our tests have several important implications for the design of retrieval systems. First, coupling the embedding dimension with the index depth is a productive inductive bias because it exploits the multi-scale structure of existing MRL models without requiring additional trainable parameters or training. Second, lightweight, entity-based signals can effectively proxy the reasoning and planning typically performed by LLMs, substantially reducing query time without a corresponding loss in answer quality. Third, a performance comparable to that of graph-based pipelines can be achieved with structured retrieval, without the need for explicit KGs, entity linking and LLM-based summarization.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: Third, a performance comparable to that of graph-based pipelines can be achieved with structured retrieval, without the need for explicit KGs, entity linking and LLM-based summarization. This makes MatRAG’s approach applicable to a broad range of corpora without requiring explicit KG construction, eliminating the need for the preprocessing that theseoperationsrequire. Together, thesefindingssuggestthatthedichotomy between cheap, flat retrieval and expensive, structured retrieval can be par- 25 tially bridged by carefully co-designing the embedding strategy and the index structure. As for the MatRAG’s limitations, we observe that the entity extraction step of MatRAG relies on GLiNER [41], which can fail to identify domainspecific entities or produce inaccurate extractions on corpora with unusual terminology. Errors in this step propagate into the budget control mechanism and the re-ranking signal. Additionally, the quality of the hierarchical index depends on the density of the embedding space.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: Additionally, the quality of the hierarchical index depends on the density of the embedding space. For instance, clusters may be poorly defined on corpora with very uniform semantic distributions, reducing the discriminative value of the DAG traversal. Finally, the greedy, top-down traversal of the DAG selects the most similar cluster centroid at each level, committing irrevocably to that branch without a backtracking mechanism. An error at a coarse level, where shorter Matryoshka prefixes provide less discriminative representations, propagates downward and may exclude relevant documents from the candidate set, regardless of their similarity at finer levels. The nearest overlapping assignment mitigates this risk by ensuring that each node is reachable frompparent clusters, thus providing redundant paths through the hierarchy. However, if the correct branch is not among the selected parents of a relevant node, the traversal offers no recovery mechanism.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: Inthispaper, wehavepresentedMatRAG,ahierarchicalRAGframework for multi-hop Question Answering that leverages the structural alignment between density-based clustering and MRL. MatRAG organizes a document corpus into a DAG of clusters, associating each level with a correspondingly shorter MRL prefix dimension. This enables top-down retrieval that is dimensionality-aware and semantically structured. Unlike the multi-hop approach used by many KG-based RAGs, MatRAG employs an entity-driven iterative mechanism that controls the retrieval budget through entity counts and re-ranks candidates based on entity overlap. Furthermore, an adaptive anchoring schedule mitigates query drift by progressively increasing the weight of the original query as the budget is consumed. Experiments on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, designed to compare MatRAG with seven representative baselines, demonstrate that MatRAG consistently delivers superior retrieval and answer quality across a wide range of settings. Additionally, it reduces indexing time by orders of magnitude compared to graph-based methods and reduces query-time latency by over35.14%compared to NaiveRAG. 26 Future work will explore three main directions.

title: A Matryoshka Hierarchical RAG for Efficient Multi-Hop Question Answering
text: Additionally, it reduces indexing time by orders of magnitude compared to graph-based methods and reduces query-time latency by over35.14%compared to NaiveRAG. 26 Future work will explore three main directions. The first is predicting a query-dependent retrieval budget, which adjusts the number of retrieved documents based on the query complexity. The second direction involves learning adaptive cluster connectivity, which replaces a fixed number of parentassignmentswithahierarchythatbetterreflectsthesemanticstructureof the corpus. The third direction involves a query-dependent anchoring schedule that balances the original and expanded queries dynamically, enabling more effective exploration while preserving alignment with the question. title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Context. Architectural degradation undermines software maintainability, evolvability, and quality. However, existing research remains fragmented across measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies, limiting our understanding of how these elements relate across the degradation lifecycle. Aim. We consolidate the state of the art on architectural degradation by examining how researchers measure it, which metrics and tools support its assessment, and how existing approaches address remediation. Method. We conducted a Multivocal Literature Review of 284 peer-reviewed and grey-literature studies. We supported screening, data extraction, and classification with a locally executed LLM-assisted pipeline combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation, multi-model validation, and human adjudication. We then analyzed the resulting taxonomies and their cross-dimensional relationships. Results and Conclusions. We identified 277 measurement approaches, 357 metrics, 238 tools, and 395 remediation approaches. Research strongly concentrates on static and structural analysis, structural metrics, and detection-oriented tools. In contrast, remediation spans heterogeneous code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions and shows substantially less consolidation. Overall, the field has developed a mature diagnostic apparatus but has made less progress in connecting degradation detection with effective remediation. Our results provide a structured view of the available techniques and identify the diagnosis-remediation gap as a key direction for future research.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Software architecture underpins the long-term maintainability, modifiability, scalability, and evolvability of a system [10]. Yet as systems evolve to meet new requirements, technologies, and business constraints, their implementation inevitably drifts away from the intended design. This phenomenon,architectural degradationorerosion, gradually erodes architectural integrity and threatens sustainability [11, 21]. Degradation is rarely the result of a single poor decision. It accumulates through continuous evolution, undocumented changes, architectural violations, growing dependency complexity, and routine maintenance. Over time, systems become harder to understand, maintain, and extend, while organizations face rising costs and mounting architectural technical debt [16]. Understanding how to identify, measure, and remediate architectural degradation has therefore become a pressing research and industrial challenge. Over the past two decades, researchers have proposed a broad spectrum of techniques to tackle this challenge, including architecture conformance checking, architectural smell detection, dependency analysis, architecture recovery, software metrics, static and dynamic analysis, and, more recently, AI-assisted approaches [17, 23].

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Over the past two decades, researchers have proposed a broad spectrum of techniques to tackle this challenge, including architecture conformance checking, architectural smell detection, dependency analysis, architecture recovery, software metrics, static and dynamic analysis, and, more recently, AI-assisted approaches [17, 23]. Numerous tools support degradation assessment, and remediation strategies have been proposed at the code, architectural, organizational, and runtime levels. Despite this substantial body of work, the knowledge remains fragmented. Existing secondary studies typically examine only isolated aspects, metrics, recovery, or erosion detection, making it difficult to see how measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies relate to one another. Consequently, researchers and practitioners still lack a unified view of the architectural degradation landscape and the connections among its fundamental building blocks. To fill this gap, we conducted a Multivocal Literature Review (MLR) [9] that synthesizes evidence from both peerreviewed and grey literature.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: To fill this gap, we conducted a Multivocal Literature Review (MLR) [9] that synthesizes evidence from both peerreviewed and grey literature. To handle the large-scale analysis, we employed an LLM-assisted pipeline based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), multi-model validation, and human adjudication. Beyond independently classifying the existing literature, we connect the resulting taxonomies through cross-dimensional and maturity analyses, providing an integrated perspective of the architectural degradation ecosystem. This study makes the following contributions: •a comprehensive multivocal literature review on architectural degradation; •four evidence-based taxonomies; •an integrated and maturity analysis of the research landscape. Our synthesis reveals a striking convergence: the community has built a mature, structurally focused diagnostic apparatus, static analysis, structural design metrics, and detection-oriented tooling dominate the field. In contrast, remediation remains fragmented across code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions, and the transition from detecting degradation to acting on it is still comparatively immature.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: In contrast, remediation remains fragmented across code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions, and the transition from detecting degradation to acting on it is still comparatively immature. These findings offer researchers a structured agenda for closing the diagnosis–remediation gap and give practitioners an evidence-based map of the techniques available for assessing and managing architectural degradation. Paper structure:Section 2 describes the background and the related works, while Section 3 the design of this study. Section 4 presents the obtained results and Section 5 discusses them. Section 6 identifies some threats to validity while Section 7 draws the conclusion.

This section summarizes the most relevant contributions in this area, covering a variety of approaches and findings. The existing work addresses both conceptual frameworks and practical solutions, with a particular focus on improving recovery techniques and mitigating associated risks. However, a comprehensive understanding of architectural degradation requires examining not only how it is detected and measured, but also the tools that support its assessment and the strategies proposed for its remediation. In this regard, there remains a need for a comprehensive investigation integrating these complementary dimensions of architectural degradation. To show how research in this area has evolved, we present the selected studies in chronological order. The earliest review was conducted by De Silva and Balasubramaniam [23], while the most recent, to the best of our knowledge, is by Baabad et al. [3]. The primary objective of each study is summarized in Table 1.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: The primary objective of each study is summarized in Table 1. The study by De Silva and Balasubramaniam [23] provides structured overviews of architectural erosion, classifying existing techniques into prevention, minimization, and repair. The authors analyze the methodologies, tools, and processes associated with each category, emphasizing that architectural erosion cannot be effectively addressed through a single strategy. Instead, they advocate for a combined approach that integrates multiple techniques to manage the problem more comprehensively. Herold et al. [10] conducted a literature review focusing on empirical studies related to architectural degradation and consistency checking. The objective was to assess the current state of research and identify areas that have been underexplored. Their findings indicate that many proposed solutions to remediate architectural degradation rely on case studies with limited generalizability. As a result, the authors highlight the need for more rigorous empirical validation, including controlled experiments and large-scale studies, to better understand the effectiveness of these approaches.

The work by [30] examines the evolution of architecture recovery techniques, particularly the transition from manual to automated approaches. The study reflects the growing influence of industry demands for faster development cycles, which has driven the need for more efficient recovery methods. The authors emphasize the importance of maintaining architectural integrity in rapidly evolving systems and suggest that future research should focus on automated and semi-automated solutions. title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: [24] carried out a mapping study investigating the application of architecture recovery techniques in software product lines (SPLs). The study highlights the challenges of adapting approaches designed for single systems to the more complex SPL context. In particular, it identifies limitations in the handling of shared assets and the management of variability. The findings suggest that existing techniques do not adequately address architectural degradation in SPLs, especially in systems that evolve from cloned or ad hoc codebases and accumulate technical debt over time. Baabad et al. [2] reviewed the architectural degradation in open-source software, identifying key contributing factors such as frequent modifications, rapid system evolution, and limited architectural awareness among developers. The study also highlights common indicators of degradation, including code smells and architectural smells, and emphasizes the need for more research to better understand these causes and improve remediation strategies. Li et al. [17] conducted a survey to explore architectural erosion from a practitioner’s perspective.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: [17] conducted a survey to explore architectural erosion from a practitioner’s perspective. The study aims to understand how developers perceive, identify, and manage erosion in practice. The results indicate that architectural erosion is viewed as a structural issue affecting software quality, driven by both technical and organizational factors. Practitioners typically recognize erosion through its symptoms and attempt to mitigate its impact, although the study highlights the need for stronger empirical support for existing tools and techniques. Finally, Baabad et al. [3] presented a mapping study focusing on metrics for architectural degradation. The study categorizes existing metrics and demonstrates their role in identifying architectural decay. However, it also highlights the need for further investigation into how these metrics function and how effectively they capture different aspects of degradation. Although previous secondary studies have examined architectural erosion, recovery techniques, degradation metrics, and practitioner perceptions, they generally address these dimensions separately.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Although previous secondary studies have examined architectural erosion, recovery techniques, degradation metrics, and practitioner perceptions, they generally address these dimensions separately. None provides an integrated synthesis connecting measurement approaches, metrics, tool support, and remediation strategies across the architectural degradation lifecycle. Our work addresses this gap through a multivocal literature review that combines academic and practitioner evidence and analyzes both the individual dimensions and their cross-dimensional relationships. In summary, existing secondary studies provide valuable but largely dimension-specific views of architectural degradation. What remains missing is a synthesis that jointly examines how degradation is measured, which metrics operationalize it, which tools support its assessment, and which strategies are available for remediation. Our study addresses this gap by integrating these four dimensions and examining their relationships across the architectural degradation lifecycle.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Architectural degradation has been investigated through a broad range of approaches, including metric-based analyses, architecture conformance checking, smell detection, dependency analysis, graph-based techniques, and machine learning methods. However, these approaches have been proposed independently, making it difficult to obtain a comprehensive view of the available solutions and their characteristics. This analysis provides researchers and practitioners with a consolidated overview of the current state of the art and reveals areas requiring further methodological advances. RQ2 Which metrics have been considered for measuring architectural degradation? RQ2 addresses the metrics used to assess software architectural degradation. Architectural degradation cannot be directly observed or quantified. Instead, existing studies rely on a variety of proxy metrics that capture structural properties, architectural symptoms, software evolution, and quality-related consequences. Despite the extensive body of research, there is currently no consolidated understanding of which metrics are adopted, which architectural dimensions they capture, or whether a common measurement framework has emerged.

RQ3 aims to identify and classify the tools proposed for assessing architectural degradation, analyzing their supported functionalities, underlying approaches, and level of automation. This pipeline supports the extraction and classification of measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies at scale while preserving human oversight throughout the process. Importantly, our aim is not to replace established empirical review methods, but to support their application at a larger scale while maintaining methodological rigor and traceability. In our study, we analyzed peer-reviewed and grey literature on software architectural degradation and extracted information on measurement approaches, metrics, supporting tools, and remediation strategies.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: In our study, we analyzed peer-reviewed and grey literature on software architectural degradation and extracted information on measurement approaches, metrics, supporting tools, and remediation strategies. Our methodology followed five main steps: (1) Using a large reasoning model to make a decision about papers inclusion and data extraction; (2) Validation of the output with three LLMs and human validation; (3) Clean and unify the extracted data; Manuscript submitted to ACM 12 Noman Ahmad, Ruoyu Su, Matteo Esposito, Andrea Janes, Valentina Lenarduzzi, and Davide Taibi (4) Categorize the extracted data from the papers by using LLM; (5) Analyze co-occurrence patterns and map relationships

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: LRM/LLM Model Roles:We assigned a unique role to each model based on its responsibility in the data analysis pipeline as follows (Table 7): • Large Reasoning Model (LRM):Marco-o1 is responsible to extract the required information. For each prompt, it receives input data (e.g., title/abstract, full paper), it makes decision first of all about title and abstract selection and then full read the selected papers and later on classifies the data into categories, and provides information. Its output formed the basis for further verification and was referred to as LRM responses throughout the study. • Validation Models (V1/V2/V3):Llama, Mistral-NeMo, and Qwen are used for validation task. They receive the similar input as the LRM and used to evaluate against the LRM’s reasoning and output. Prompting Techniques:We applied prompt engineering strategies to steer LRM/LLM in classifying approaches to measure and remediate software architectural degradation.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Prompting Techniques:We applied prompt engineering strategies to steer LRM/LLM in classifying approaches to measure and remediate software architectural degradation. Prior research indicates that in-context learning via chat-based prompting can achieve performance comparable to or exceeding that of fine-tuning, while avoiding its higher computational cost [6]. In our setup, each prompt comprised two elements: asystem message, which defined the assistant’s role and specified the required output structure, and auser message, which supplied the contextual input (e.g title/abstract). The model was instructed to produce a structured JSON output including: •The predicted category; •A briefdescription; •The correspondingreasoning. We employed a few-shot learning approach combined with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [28] to encourage more transparent and accurate classification. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG):.We implemented a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mechanism into our pipeline for both full-document processing. RAG enhances the model’s input with relevant external knowledge by retrieving semantically similar, previously labeled instances from the dataset using embedding-based similarity search.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: RAG enhances the model’s input with relevant external knowledge by retrieving semantically similar, previously labeled instances from the dataset using embedding-based similarity search. In our case, scientific PDFs exceed typical model context limits, each document was first converted into text, segmented into overlapping chunks, and indexed using embedding-based similarity search (FAISS). The model was then instructed to generate a structured JSON output containing one concise answer per category. This approach enables efficient processing of long documents while ensuring that classification decisions are evidence-based, context-aware, and less prone to hallucination. Running LRM/LLM:.For executing this big scale analysis, we CSC’s Mahti supercomputer, using vLLM to serve the LRM/LLM for large-scale inference1. Mahti is a high-performance computing platform intended for computationally and data-intensive research, providing more than 180,000 CPU cores connected through a fast interconnect network. Our jobs leveraged up to four NVIDIA A100 GPUs, ensuring high-speed and memory-efficient inference to process large volumes of data effectively.

text: Our jobs leveraged up to four NVIDIA A100 GPUs, ensuring high-speed and memory-efficient inference to process large volumes of data effectively. We employed deterministic decoding (temperature = 0, max_tokens = 1900) with a 1http://csc.fi Manuscript submitted to ACM Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate 13 strict no-hallucination JSON prompt to ensure reproducible, evidence-grounded extraction and to minimize stochastic variability. Human Validation:Since no previous study reported findings on the accuracy of LLMs for the task at hand, we designed a validation involving three human experts mimicking the LLM validator’s roles. The goal was to assess the quality and correctness of the model-generated outputs and to determine whether the validation models provided consistent judgments. Our validation followed a three-step protocol. • One expert independently reviewed the same input provided to the LRM and the three validation models (V1–V3), and manually evaluated the correctness of each model’s motivation.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Our validation followed a three-step protocol. • One expert independently reviewed the same input provided to the LRM and the three validation models (V1–V3), and manually evaluated the correctness of each model’s motivation. For each case, the expert indicated whether they agreed or disagreed with the LRM’s motivation, noted the majority decision among the validation models, and identified the models they considered correct. • A second expert repeated the same evaluation independently and documented their level of agreement with the first expert’s judgments. • In cases of disagreement between the first two reviewers, a third expert was brought in to independently assess the same outputs. Final decisions were made through majority voting among the three validators. Table 7.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: The extracted fields were defined before the extraction process and were directly mapped to the research questions. Table 8 summarizes the extracted data items, their purpose, and their relationship with each research question. Each primary study was processed using the LRM/LLM-based extraction pipeline (Section 3.3). The full text of each paper was provided to the LRM together with prompts specifically designed to extract the information required for the review. The LRM generated structured JSON outputs containing the extracted information, which were automatically converted into CSV files to facilitate subsequent analysis. To improve the reliability of the extracted data, the generated outputs were validated using the multi-model validation process (Section 3.3). Whenever inconsistencies or lowconfidence extractions were detected, the corresponding studies were manually inspected and the extracted information was corrected accordingly. As summarized in Table 8, we extracted information regarding measurement approaches, architectural degradation metrics, supporting tools, and remediation strategies.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: We classified the remediation approaches into seven categories according to the level and timing of their intervention. Figure 6 and Table 13 show that the literature emphasizes corrective actions at the code, organizational, and architectural levels, while it devotes less attention to less conventional forms of remediation. Code-Level Repairrepresents the most common remediation category and appears in51.4%of the primary studies. Refactoring and Restructuring drives this category and appears in 39.4% of the studies WL7, WL11, WL17, WL20, WL24, WL25,GL275, GL279, GL280, GL282. Smell and Violation Resolution accounts for 6.7% WL6, WL27, WL33, WL35, WL36, WL38, WL39, WL44,GL269, GL273, while Dependency and Modularity Improvement accounts for 5.3% WL9, WL15, WL78, WL86, WL249, WL251. These approaches modify the implementation to improve its internal structure while preserving its expected external behavior. They include operations such as extracting methods or classes, moving elements across modules, reducing dependencies, and reorganizing package or module boundaries. Process & Organizational Remediationfollows closely and appears in49.3%of the studies.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: detecting and addressing it [23?]. The evidence synthesized in this review suggests that progress has not been uniform across the architectural degradation lifecycle. The literature has advanced considerably in understanding how degradation can be identified, whereas substantially less agreement exists on how it should be prevented, remediated, and continuously managed. This imbalance appears consistently across all four research questions. Measurement approaches, metric families, and tooling exhibit a high degree of convergence, indicating that the community largely shares a common understanding of how architectural degradation should be assessed. In contrast, remediation strategies remain fragmented across technical, architectural, and organizational interventions, with no comparable consensus emerging. More than a decade ago, De Silva and Balasubramaniam argued that effectively controlling architectural erosion requires combining prevention, detection, and restoration strategies rather than relying on isolated technical solutions [23]. The evidence collected in this review suggests that this objective has not yet been fully achieved.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: The evidence collected in this review suggests that this objective has not yet been fully achieved. While the literature provides a mature ecosystem of techniques for recognizing degradation, considerably less attention has been devoted to understanding how different remediation strategies should be selected, coordinated, and sustained over time. Manuscript submitted to ACM 24 Noman Ahmad, Ruoyu Su, Matteo Esposito, Andrea Janes, Valentina Lenarduzzi, and Davide Taibi Perhaps the most consistent finding is the strongstructural biasthat characterizes the literature. Static & Structural Analysis dominates the measurement approaches, while Structural Design Metrics appear in more than 90% of the primary studies. This observation agrees with previous work showing that architectural degradation is primarily identified through structural symptoms, architectural anomalies, and conformance violations rather than runtime evidence [3, 19]. Our results indicate that this predominance extends beyond the choice of metrics. Structural reasoning shapes the entire assessment process, influencing how degradation is measured, how evidence is collected, and how supporting tools are designed.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Structural reasoning shapes the entire assessment process, influencing how degradation is measured, how evidence is collected, and how supporting tools are designed. By comparison, relatively few studies investigate degradation through system execution. Dynamic analysis, runtime metrics, and runtime-aware remediation remain markedly underrepresented. This imbalance is understandable because structural artifacts are easier to collect, deterministic to analyze, and supported by mature tooling. However, architectural degradation is inherently an evolutionary phenomenon. It emerges through continuous software evolution, changing requirements, operational pressures, and accumulated design decisions rather than from static structure alone. Consequently, assessment approaches centred primarily on structural evidence are likely to identify degradation only after its effects have already materialized within the implemented architecture. This predominance of structural assessment contrasts with the broader view that architectural quality should be continuously preserved throughout software evolution rather than periodically evaluated [14]. This interpretation also complements the observations of Li et al.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: This interpretation also complements the observations of Li et al. [?], who argue that architectural erosion should not be viewed solely as a structural phenomenon but also as the result of organizational and evolutionary processes. While the literature increasingly acknowledges these broader causes, the methods used to assess degradation remain overwhelmingly centred on structural properties. The evidence therefore reveals a disconnect between how architectural degradation is conceptualized and how it is empirically investigated. The end-to-end paths reported in Figure 2 reinforce this interpretation. The most informative observation is not that the dominant path represents only 18 studies, but that nearly all dominant paths follow the same sequence of static analysis, structural metrics, and detection tools before diverging during remediation. This remarkable stability indicates that methodological diversity is concentrated almost entirely after degradation has been identified.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: This remarkable stability indicates that methodological diversity is concentrated almost entirely after degradation has been identified. In other words, the community has largely converged on how degradation should be observed, while substantially different views remain on how corrective actions should be designed, prioritized, and combined. This pattern also clarifies the conclusions of previous secondary studies. De Silva and Balasubramaniam organized the literature into complementary prevention, detection, and restoration strategies [23], whereas Li et al. highlighted the broad spectrum of techniques proposed to detect and address architectural erosion [18]. The evidence synthesized here suggests that this diversity is not uniformly distributed across the degradation lifecycle. Instead, it emerges primarily after degradation has been diagnosed. Before that point, the literature exhibits a remarkably stable methodological pipeline centred on structural assessment. The principal challenge therefore appears to have shifted from improving degradation detection toward understanding how different remediation strategies should interact to preserve architectural integrity throughout software evolution. 1. Key Take Away.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Key Take Away. Architectural degradation research has reached methodological maturity in diagnosis but not in remediation.The literature consistently converges on static analysis, structural metrics, and detection tools to identify degradation. In contrast, remediation remains fragmented across code-level, architectural, and organizational Manuscript submitted to ACM Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate 25 interventions, suggesting that future advances are more likely to arise from integrating corrective strategies than from proposing additional detection techniques.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: A second concern emerging from the findings is the clearimbalance between diagnosis and intervention. The literature provides a rich ecosystem of approaches for identifying architectural degradation, including structural metrics, rule checking, smell detection, and dedicated analysis tools. By contrast, considerably fewer studies investigate how degradation should be addressed once it has been detected. This imbalance is particularly evident in the tooling landscape, where Detection & Analysis Tools largely outnumber Remediation-Support Tools. The evidence therefore suggests that the community has invested substantially more effort in answering the question“Is the architecture degrading?”than“What should be done next?” The remediation landscape reveals an additional level of fragmentation. Code-Level Repair, Architecture-Level Repair, and Process & Organizational Remediation all receive substantial attention, yet they are rarely investigated as complementary components of the same intervention strategy. Most studies focus on one level of action while treating the others as external concerns. However, architectural degradation rarely originates from a single cause.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: However, architectural degradation rarely originates from a single cause. It accumulates through design decisions, implementation shortcuts, evolving requirements, and organizational constraints acting simultaneously. This observation closely resembles the challenges discussed in the Architectural Technical Debt literature, where long-term architectural quality depends on continuously managing the consequences of local design decisions rather than periodically correcting accumulated problems [15, 20]. The unexpectedly high presence of Recovery & Reverse-Engineering tools reinforces this interpretation. Rather than preventing degradation during software evolution, a considerable portion of the literature concentrates on reconstructing architectural knowledge after it has already been lost. Similar observations motivated previous work on architecture-preserving refactorings, where architectural recovery is viewed as a prerequisite for restoring architectural integrity rather than preventing degradation in the first place [27]. Together, these findings suggest that a significant part of the literature remains inherently reactive, addressing degradation after architectural knowledge has already deteriorated. Another notable observation concerns predictive approaches.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Another notable observation concerns predictive approaches. Despite the increasing availability of software repositories, architectural histories, and development analytics, Machine Learning and Prediction remain among the least represented measurement approaches, while AI/ML-based tooling also occupies only a limited portion of the landscape. Rather than indicating a lack of interest in artificial intelligence, these results suggest that predictive architectural degradation remains an emerging research direction. Existing studies continue to rely predominantly on structural indicators and threshold-based reasoning, whereas comparatively little attention has been devoted to forecasting degradation trajectories before architectural symptoms become observable. This gap appears particularly significant considering that architectural degradation is inherently progressive and cumulative, making early intervention substantially more valuable than late diagnosis. 2. Key Take Away.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Tables 15 and 16 report the classification, while Figures 7 and 8 illustrate the distributions. Together, these measures describe the coverage and breadth of the literature, without directly establishing effectiveness, adoption, or methodological maturity. The concentration of approaches, metrics, and tools aroundstructural assessmentgives researchers several ways to examine dependencies, modular boundaries, and architectural violations. Far fewer approaches explicitly investigate how these properties change: the catalogue contains 78 static and structural approaches, compared with seven evolutionary and historical approaches. This difference highlights an opportunity to connect structural observations across successive versions and examine when architectural changes indicate deterioration. Static techniques can contribute to this investigation, provided that their application and interpretation account for the system’s evolution. Choosing among the available structural techniques requires understandingwhat additional evidence each contributes. Techniques may examine similar properties while relying on different assumptions, inputs, or thresholds. Combining them may broaden the assessment, but it may also reproduce the same information through several indicators.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Combining them may broaden the assessment, but it may also reproduce the same information through several indicators. Comparative evaluations would help distinguish complementary measurements from redundant ones and establish whether their conclusions remain consistent across systems and stages of evolution. The breadth of remediation extends across implementation, architecture, and development practices, with 66 codelevel, 64 architectural, and 65 organizational strategies. This range challenges a general characterization of remediation as immature and makesintervention selectiona more precise concern. An architectural violation, for example, may require both a technical correction and changes to the practices that allowed it to recur. The catalogue identifies possible responses, but does not establish which combinations are appropriate under particular conditions. Studies connecting the diagnosed problem to the intervention rationale, implementation costs, and outcomes over subsequent releases would provide stronger guidance for these decisions.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Establishing whether knowledge is accumulating requires examining how studies reuse earlier techniques, test their assumptions, and compare their findings. A small catalogue supported by repeated validation may offer more dependable guidance than a larger catalogue whose techniques remain difficult to compare. The 51 runtime and operational metrics and 45 evolutionary and change metrics provide varied ways to examine dimensions that receive less attention than structural assessment. Their contribution to degradation management depends on whether they informactionable architectural decisions. Evaluations could trace whether changes in these indicators reveal a problem, influence the choice of an intervention, and capture its subsequent effects. This requires distinguishing execution behaviour from architectural change across versions: each provides different evidence, and neither alone establishes how degradation develops. Comparative studies would make extensive catalogues easier to use by clarifying technique selection and applicability. For smaller catalogues, evaluations should establish whether existing techniques adequately cover the relevant degradation phenomena and produce reliable findings.

Followingthe connection from measurement to intervention and sustained outcomeswould address both needs, showing how the available contributions support degradation management in practice. This would provide empirical support for the combined use of prevention, detection, and repair advocated by previous reviews [18, 23]. 3. Key Take Away. The breadth of available techniques makes their selection and integration a central research challenge. Structural assessment and remediation offer extensive catalogues, but their size alone does not establish maturity or effectiveness. Comparative evaluations are needed to clarify which techniques provide complementary evidence, when particular interventions are appropriate, and whether their benefits persist over time. Shared benchmarks Manuscript submitted to ACM Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate 29 and longitudinal datasets could support these evaluations, strengtheningthe connection between diagnosis, corrective action, and sustained architectural improvement.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Our review brings together techniques for observing architectural degradation and strategies for addressing it, while showing a stronger emphasis on structural assessment within measurement approaches and tooling. We therefore identify a practical need to distinguisharchitectural anomalies from evidence of architectural degradation. Although coupling, complexity, or a detected smell can identify a concern, establishing degradation requires examining its relationship with architectural intent and its consequences for system evolution. Conformance checks and recovered architectural views can support this interpretation; however, recovered views describe the implemented structure and may reproduce the dependencies under investigation. We consequently recommend distinguishing recovered structure from intended constraints before using it to guide corrective action. Through RQ4, we identified strategies addressing both software structure and development practices, which motivates connectingarchitectural repair with measures that prevent recurrence. While refactoring may remove an unwanted dependency, architectural rules, decision documentation, and review responsibilities may help prevent its reintroduction.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: While refactoring may remove an unwanted dependency, architectural rules, decision documentation, and review responsibilities may help prevent its reintroduction. We therefore recommend comparing technical repair alone with repair accompanied by changes to architectural guidance or development practices. Such comparisons would establish whether organizational measures reduce recurring violations sufficiently to justify their cost, thereby giving empirical substance to combined erosioncontrol strategies [23]. Evaluating those interventions also requires distinguishingmeasurements of architectural deterioration from descriptions of structural change. Although RQ 2 identifies a broad catalogue of structural metrics, changes in coupling or complexity do not necessarily imply worsening maintainability or increasing change effort. We thus propose examining when metric changes coincide with architectural violations, changes spreading across component boundaries, or more costly modifications, while comparing cases in which similar structural changes support legitimate evolution. The resulting evidence would help determine both when a measurement warrants intervention and whether an observed improvement indicates successful remediation.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: The resulting evidence would help determine both when a measurement warrants intervention and whether an observed improvement indicates successful remediation. Across RQ3 and RQ4, we observed an emphasis on detection-oriented tooling alongside a broad range of remediation strategies; we consequently identifyexplicit links between degradation symptoms and corrective actionsas a research priority. While diagnostic evidence identifies the concern, selecting a repair also requires considering architectural constraints and expected evolution costs. We therefore propose investigating how those factors justify particular interventions, so that supporting tools can explain the rationale and trade-offs behind their recommendations. Evaluations could then establish whether the recommended actions address the diagnosed degradation without transferring dependencies or maintenance burdens elsewhere [15]. 4. Architectural degradation should increasingly be managed as a continuous architectural governance activity rather than a periodic assessment task. Future research should prioritize runtime-aware assessment, decision-support for remediation, and predictive architectural governance to complement the mature ecosystem of structural analysis and detection techniques. title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: This section discusses the potential threats to validity following the categories proposed by Wohlin et al. [29]. Construct Validity.Construct validity concerns whether the collected data accurately represents the phenomenon under investigation [29]. We investigated approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation techniques related to architectural degradation across both peer-reviewed and grey literature. However, architectural degradation lacks a universally accepted terminology, and closely related concepts such as erosion, decay, drift, aging, technical debt, and architecture conformance frequently overlap. In particular, several primary studies treat architecture conformance as evidence or a proxy of architectural degradation, whereas others consider it a distinct research topic. Consequently, some included studies may operationalize degradation differently, potentially affecting the resulting taxonomy. Moreover, our LLM-supported extraction and classification pipeline may have interpreted ambiguous descriptions differently from human experts, particularly in heterogeneous grey literature. Our manual validation also showed that one validation model (Qwen) consistently achieved lower agreement than the other models for several extraction and classification tasks.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Our manual validation also showed that one validation model (Qwen) consistently achieved lower agreement than the other models for several extraction and classification tasks. Rather than relying on a single model, we mitigated these threats by defining explicit inclusion criteria, grounding model responses through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), validating every extraction using three independent LLMs, identifying disagreements through model consensus, and resolving them through human adjudication and majority voting. Internal Validity.Internal validity concerns whether the reported findings originate from the analyzed evidence rather than methodological artifacts [29]. Our study relied on LLMs to support study selection, information extraction, and thematic classification. Different LLMs may encode different prior knowledge, reasoning strategies, or alignment policies, potentially producing different classifications for ambiguous cases. Likewise, prompt formulation and category consolidation may influence the final taxonomy.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Likewise, prompt formulation and category consolidation may influence the final taxonomy. We reduced them by assigning specialized roles to the models, validating every output through a multi-model consensus process, performing several rounds of iterative refinement before final validation, and involving multiple independent human validators to resolve disagreements through majority voting. External Validity.External validity concerns the generalizability of the findings beyond the analyzed dataset [ 29]. We analyzed 284 primary studies retrieved from multiple scientific databases together with grey literature, providing broad coverage of both academic and industrial perspectives. Nevertheless, our dataset only includes English-language publications indexed by the selected databases and search engines that were available at the time of the search. Furthermore, grey literature varies substantially in reporting quality and methodological rigor. Although we applied identical inclusion criteria, extraction procedures, and validation processes to both peer-reviewed and grey literature, some industrial practices, non-English publications, or emerging trends may remain underrepresented.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: Although we applied identical inclusion criteria, extraction procedures, and validation processes to both peer-reviewed and grey literature, some industrial practices, non-English publications, or emerging trends may remain underrepresented. Future updates of the multivocal literature review may therefore identify additional approaches, metrics, tools, or remediation techniques. Conclusion Validity.Conclusion validity concerns whether the conclusions are adequately supported by the available evidence [29]. Our study synthesizes recurring patterns across 284 primary studies rather than establishing statistical or causal relationships. Therefore, frequently reported approaches, metrics, tools, or remediation strategies should not be interpreted as evidence of superior effectiveness, but as the most consistently reported evidence in the literature. The use of LLMs introduces additional threats due to the inherent variability and limited transparency of their outputs. We mitigated these threats through local inference with fixed model versions, deterministic decoding (temperature = 0), fixed parameters, RAG, and validation using three independent LLMs followed by human majority voting.

We also documented the complete pipeline and provide a replication package. Nevertheless, different models or Manuscript submitted to ACM Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate 31 execution environments may produce minor variations; reproducibility should therefore be considered at the level of taxonomies, categories, and aggregate findings rather than exact outputs.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: This paper presented a Multivocal Literature Review of 284 primary studies, delivering the first integrated view of architectural degradation across four dimensions: measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies. The resulting taxonomies and cross-dimensional analysis reveal a field that has matured impressively atdetecting degradation, static analysis, structural metrics, and detection tools dominate the landscape, but remains fragmented and comparatively immature when it comes toactingon what is detected. Remediation strategies are scattered across code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions with no shared vision, and the tooling ecosystem offers extensive support for diagnosis yet very little for deciding or executing corrective actions. The central implication is clear: the next generation of research must shift from building yet more detection techniques toward closing the diagnosis–remediation gap.Priorities include decision-support frameworks that help practitioners select and prioritize remediation strategies, runtime-aware and predictive approaches that catch degradation before it solidifies, and continuous architectural governance that treats degradation management as an ongoing process rather than a periodic assessment.

title: Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate
text: The central implication is clear: the next generation of research must shift from building yet more detection techniques toward closing the diagnosis–remediation gap.Priorities include decision-support frameworks that help practitioners select and prioritize remediation strategies, runtime-aware and predictive approaches that catch degradation before it solidifies, and continuous architectural governance that treats degradation management as an ongoing process rather than a periodic assessment. For practitioners, the evidence synthesized here provides an actionable map of what is available today and where the blind spots remain. Architectural degradation is not a solved problem, but the path forward is now visible. We hope the taxonomies, maturity analysis, and conceptual framework offered in this work serve both as a reference for future research and as a practical foundation for building the next generation of intelligent, continuous, and automated degradation-management solutions. title: Evaluating Biomedical Reranking for LLM-Based Question Answering over Longitudinal Clinical Notes
text: Patient-specific clinical question answering requires locating the right evidence within long, heterogeneous longitudinal clinical records in which relevant facts may be scattered across encounters, repeated in copied-forward notes, or expressed using different clinical terminology. We evaluated whether biomedical reranking can improve evidence selection and downstream answer quality in a locally deployed retrieval-augmented generation pipeline for longitudinal clinical notes. The pipeline combines PubMedBERT dense retrieval, BM25 lexical retrieval, weighted reciprocal-rank fusion, and MedCPT cross-encoder reranking. Across 1,000 open- and closed-ended question-answer pairs from a cohort of 200 bariatric surgery patients, reranking increased exact source-chunk retrieval within the top 10 items, Hit@10 from 46.6% to 60.6% and mean reciprocal rank from 0.2371 to 0.3252. With Qwen3-8B generation, local judge-assessed answer correctness increased from 44.8% to 48.6%. These results show that biomedical reranking can improve the placement of relevant clinical evidence within a limited context window, although gains in retrieval do not translate proportionally into gains in answer correctness.

title: Evaluating Biomedical Reranking for LLM-Based Question Answering over Longitudinal Clinical Notes
text: Patient-specific clinical question answering (QA) differs from general medical QA because the required evidence is often buried within a single patient’s longitudinal record rather than contained in model pretraining. Relevant facts may be distributed across encounters, repeated in copiedforward notes, or expressed using different clinical terminology. This creates a retrieval problem in which the system must identify the most informative evidence from a large, redundant record while operating within a lim ited context window. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides a mechanism for supplying patient-specific evidence to a language model, but the usefulness of the final answer depends heavily on which passages are retrieved and how they are ranked. Towards this goal, MIRAGE benchmark and MedRAG toolkit were introduced to systematically evaluate retrieval configurations for the medical QA [1]. In longitudinal clinical records, this distinction is particularly important because retrieving the relevant evidence and correctly interpreting that evidence are separate stages of the pipeline.

title: Evaluating Biomedical Reranking for LLM-Based Question Answering over Longitudinal Clinical Notes
text: In longitudinal clinical records, this distinction is particularly important because retrieving the relevant evidence and correctly interpreting that evidence are separate stages of the pipeline. Dense retrieval can capture semantically related text, whereas lexical retrieval rewards direct term overlap. These complementary signals can be combined using reciprocalrank fusion (RRF) [2], after which a cross encoder can jointly score the question and candidate passage. MedCPT provides a biomedical retrieval and reranking framework trained from PubMed search interactions [3]. Recent work has extended retrieval augmentation to electronic health record applications beyond general medical QA. RAG was applied to EHR summarization and clinical information extraction [4], while RAM-EHR was introduced to augment clinical prediction with retrieved medical knowledge [5]. Recent studies have further examined RAG for biomedical applications, longitudinal EHR reasoning, factual -aware medical QA, and evidence-grounded patient QA [8]-[12].

title: Evaluating Biomedical Reranking for LLM-Based Question Answering over Longitudinal Clinical Notes
text: Recent studies have further examined RAG for biomedical applications, longitudinal EHR reasoning, factual -aware medical QA, and evidence-grounded patient QA [8]-[12]. These studies demonstrate the broader value of retrieval augmentation, but do not directly evaluate whether biomedical cross-encoder reranking improves evidence of selection for patient-specific question answering over longitudinal clinical notes. We evaluate this approach using a frozen set of 1,000 QA pairs generated from 200 bariatric surgery patients, with retrieval restricted to each patient’s longitudinal record and clinical inference performed locally. This work makes three contributions: 1) evaluates biomedical cross -encoder reranking for longitudinal clinical QA, 2) quantifies the relationship between improved evidence retrieval and downstream answer correctness, including separate analysis of open- and closed-ended QA, and 3) demonstrates a fully local, patient-restricted RAG evaluation incorporating retrieval, generation, and identifier screening.

text: An overview of the proposed method is presented in Figure 1, with details about each component in the following text. 2.1 Dense and lexical candidate generation. Questions and retrieval chunks were encoded using NeuML’s PubMedBERT base embeddings checkpoint through Sentence Transformers [6]. The 768-dimensional vectors are normalized to unit length. Dense retrieval used a FAISS inner-product index within each patient’s corpus, yielding cosine-similarity rankings. Cached corpus embeddings were verified against the corpus; both contained 71,289 rows with matching source-identifier ordering. Lexical retrieval used the BM25Okapi implementation from the rank_bm25 Python package, based on the Okapi BM25 ranking function [13]. Text was lowercased and tokenized into alphanumeric sequences using the regular expression [a-z 0-9] +. Each retriever returned up to 30 candidates, producing a union of at most 60 unique source chunks.
